Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe

Richmond Sin Jing Xuan    Peilin Feng    Wenbin Wang    Soujanya Poria Affiliation: DeCLaRe Lab, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore
November 24, 2026
Abstract
Abstract

AI agents working on long tasks often stop too soon and commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior often called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. At every turn, the agent decides whether to take a further step or to commit to an answer. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer. It does not show which turns helped, and it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator knows the rules linking the hidden answer to the evidence, so it can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which takes this posterior as the belief supported by the evidence. RLVB rewards the agent for taking further steps while this belief still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward depends only on the evidence the agent has gathered and needs no judge, critic or reward model. It never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action, although the update trains this line together with the action. We also introduce Pro-Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window and must decide when it has enough visual evidence to commit. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average and by 10.4% with expectation maximization (EM) as the learner. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. To find where this gain comes from, we group the answers by the evidence the agent has when it answers. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. For every method, 66 to 92% of the answers given with sufficient evidence are correct. The accuracy gain of the trained agent therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence, while at the same level of evidence its answers are no more accurate than those of the base model. The belief line shows how the trained agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model with the same line. Over all turns, its line is not consistently more exact than that of the base model, and each of its steps adds about as much evidence as a step of the base model. Because the trained agent acts on its belief, we expect better reading of the evidence to translate into better answers.

1 Introduction

Agents that work over long horizons are now used in games, embodied settings, and other interactive environments (Yao et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025b). Such an agent must keep working until it has gathered sufficient evidence to act (Bajcsy, 1988; Das et al., 2018). However, current agents often stop too early (Laban et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Cuadron et al., 2025) and answer with a guess. This behavior is called laziness (Ma and Liu, 2025). In the cups task in figure 1, the agent lifts one cup at a time to find a hidden object. After two lifts, the evidence is not yet sufficient because the object could still be under either of two cups. The next action should therefore lift another cup instead of guessing. In our experiments, the base models often guess even after they write that several cups remain possible.

At every turn, an evidence-seeking agent should keep a belief that matches the evidence. It should take steps aimed at what this belief leaves open. It should commit only when the belief identifies the answer. Knowing how much one knows and acting on it is called metacognition (Flavell, 1979). Metacognition has two parts: monitoring what one knows and controlling what one does with it (Nelson and Narens, 1990). Language models can often recognize what they know (Kadavath et al., 2022). However, the base models in our evaluations commit too early, even though our prompts tell them to commit only once the evidence identifies the answer. When they write a belief line before each action, they commit at 3 to 68% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and this belief line still names several answers. They often state that the answer remains open and commit anyway. These models do not act on what their own belief line states. A check in the harness that rejects the first answer does not solve this problem, because the harness cannot read the observations, as section 4.6 shows. Whether the evidence determines the answer depends on what the agent has observed. Only the agent reads these observations. The agent’s own belief can therefore guide each decision once the agent learns to act on it. We call an agent reliable when its answers are both correct and backed by sufficient evidence, because a user who receives an answer usually cannot check how the agent reached it. Training an agent to make this decision reliably over a long horizon is a central problem in agentic reinforcement learning (RL).

RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a common way to train large language models on math (Shao et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025) and code (Le et al., 2022; Gehring et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025) tasks. A verifier checks the final answer and rewards the model when the answer is correct (Lambert et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Kimi Team, 2025). Recent work trains multi-turn agents with the same kind of framework (Zhou et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Feng et al., 2025). Over a long horizon, however, a reward on the final answer cannot tell which steps helped and which steps caused a failure (Minsky, 1961; Sutton and Barto, 2018). A lucky guess is reinforced as fully as an answer supported by the evidence. A careful search is penalized whenever the episode is lost. Agents also tend to answer before the evidence supports the final answer (Laban et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026) or fall back on fixed patterns that ignore the evidence (Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026b). As table 2 shows, the base models on HiddenGames give 64 to 97% of their answers before their evidence is sufficient, whether or not they write a belief line. RL with the outcome reward even lowers the accuracy of these models on average.

To credit single steps, recent work returns to the PPO framework (Schulman et al., 2017) and rewards every step with a process reward (Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2024). This reward is often given by a process reward model or an LLM judge (Cui et al., 2026; Khalifa et al., 2026). Yet the value of a step is hard to estimate, because the critic of PPO is fitted to outcomes that depend on the hidden target. As figure 2(b) shows, an LLM judge that sees the target may reward a lucky guess and penalize a correct but still uncertain belief. The critic and the judge also make training more expensive, because the critic is a second model trained next to the policy and the judge is called at every step.

Agentic RL usually trains in a sandbox simulator (Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Feng et al., 2025). This simulator knows much more than whether the final answer is correct. It knows the hidden target and what each action will reveal about it. Prior work passes this privileged information to a teacher or a critic (Pinto et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019; Choudhury and Sodhi, 2025). In tasks where the agent gathers evidence, this information lets the simulator compute the exact posterior over the hidden answer after every step. This posterior is the belief state (Åström, 1965; Kaelbling et al., 1998). The final answer is then no longer the only thing the simulator can verify. The posterior is the belief supported by the evidence. The simulator can verify it at every step, just as RLVR verifies the answer at the end. This belief shows whether the agent should take further steps or answer. This moves us from reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards to Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB).

At each turn, we give every method its full history of actions and observations. As a result, no method has to remember what it has explored. From the exact posterior, the agent learns when to commit and when to keep working. The reward also scores which step the agent chooses next, but the trained agent does not choose more informative steps than the base model, as section 4.6 shows. Before each action, the agent states the answers it still sees as possible, such as Possible: cups 2, 4. This belief line shows whether the agent thinks it has sufficient evidence. The reward never reads this line. Because the update raises the likelihood of the whole turn, it still trains the line along with the action. As section 4.6 shows, the trained agent then learns to act on the line. The turn’s reward compares the agent’s next action to the action a teacher chooses by looking ahead on the exact posterior (Howard, 1966). The reward can also score the stated belief against the posterior, but scoring the action is enough, as section 4.4 shows. The reward never pays for a guess. It depends on the evidence the agent has gathered. It does not depend on which answer happens to be correct in the episode. In figure 1, cups 2 and 4 are still possible. Lifting another cup gets a reward close to zero. Answering cup 4 gets about −7-7, whether or not the object is under cup 4. At each history, the agent samples several of its own turns and makes the higher-reward turns more likely. The learner uses either a policy gradient that compares turns within a group, as in GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), or expectation maximization (EM) (Dempster et al., 1977). RLVB needs no judge, critic or reward model because the posterior is exact.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    RLVB. We use the simulator’s privileged information to compute the exact posterior after every step. We turn this posterior into a process reward. This reward scores each action against a teacher acting on the exact posterior. The reward never reads the agent’s belief line, but the update still trains the line along with the action. After training, the agent rarely commits while it has insufficient evidence and its belief line still names several answers. The policy learns from this reward using policy gradient or EM. It needs no judge, critic or reward model.

  • •

    Experimental results. On three vision-language models and three benchmarks, RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average and by 10.4% with EM as the learner. It outperforms SFT and RL with the outcome reward in every setting. It also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge on average and uses 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours, or 4 times fewer with EM. Along with this gain, the share of answers given too early falls from 76–87% to 44–46%.

  • •

    Why the training helps. RLVB answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of episodes on the three benchmarks. The base model does so in 8%, 0.4% and 36% of episodes. Using a belief line and the exact posterior, we find that the trained agent acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns with insufficient evidence at which its belief line still names several answers. The base model with the same line commits on 3 to 68% of those turns. When it commits, the trained agent gives the answer its line names, just like the base model. Across all turns, its belief line is not consistently more exact than the base model’s. The single answers it names are often wrong. Its steps add roughly as much evidence as the base model’s. In metacognitive terms, training mainly links decision control to the agent’s own monitoring. Monitoring improves only at the states that both agents reach, where the line names a single answer too early less often. We expect a better reading of the evidence to lead to better answers.

  • •

    Pro-Worlds Benchmark. We introduce Pro-Worlds, a new benchmark of visual puzzles. The agent sees a large world only through a small window. It moves this window and must decide when it has seen enough to answer. Pro-Worlds tests this decision in visual worlds never seen in training.

2 Related Work

RL for language and vision-language agents.

RL with outcome rewards has improved the reasoning of language models (Guo et al., 2025; Kimi Team, 2025; Shao et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025). Self-training methods follow a similar idea, as they sample the model’s own rationales and keep those that reach a correct answer (Zelikman et al., 2022; Singh et al., 2024). For multi-turn agents, RAGEN (Wang et al., 2025b) finds that sparse and delayed rewards fail to reinforce the reasoning of each step. GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) obtains a finer credit by grouping the steps that share a state. VAGEN (Wang et al., 2025a) adds a turn-level reward for the agent’s estimate of the world state. These rewards still come from the outcome or from a learned estimate, while RLVB computes its rewards from the exact posterior.

Process rewards.

Process reward models score each step of a solution instead of only the final answer (Lightman et al., 2024). Most are trained on human or Monte Carlo labels, and their quality depends on how these labels are made (Zhang et al., 2025). Others learn from outcomes alone (Cui et al., 2026), reason before they judge (Khalifa et al., 2026), or derive the step reward from a regularized RL objective (Yao et al., 2026). Closer to our setting, PRInTS (Lee et al., 2026) learns a reward model for long-horizon information seeking. Our process reward is computed exactly by the environment, and it needs no reward model, no judge and no step labels.

Belief states and information gathering.

The belief state is the posterior over the hidden state. It is a sufficient statistic for acting under partial observability (Åström, 1965; Kaelbling et al., 1998). The value of an evidence-gathering action is the information gained from it (Howard, 1966; Lindley, 1956). BED-LLM (Choudhury et al., 2026) asks the questions with the highest expected information gain at test time. Bayesian teaching (Qiu et al., 2026) fine-tunes a model to imitate a Bayesian assistant. CURIO (Wan et al., 2025) and ECHO (Nath et al., 2026) reward each turn in a multi-turn interaction by how much it improves a belief over a hidden variable. Unlike these methods, RLVB uses a lookahead on the exact posterior to value the decision to stop. It also compares several turns at the same history. Agent-BRACE (Singh et al., 2026) is closest to our work. It trains an agent in text environments to state its belief as claims about the environment, each with a certainty word. Its policy acts on this belief instead of the history. An LLM judge grades these claims against the true hidden state rather than the posterior. When two answers are equally likely, the judge rewards a claim that names only the true answer, just as an outcome reward rewards a lucky guess. In RLVB, the agent is visual and states the set of answers it still sees as possible. The exact posterior scores its action and can also score this belief. As a result, the reward is verifiable and needs no judge.

3 Method

Figure 2 compares the three RL frameworks of section 1 on the cups task. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) learns from the outcome reward and gives every step the advantage of its trajectory. PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) learns from a process reward given to every step by a judge that sees the target. RLVB learns from a process reward given to every step by the exact posterior. The outcome and the judge both depend on which cup happens to hide the object in this episode, while the posterior depends only on the evidence the agent has gathered. Section 3.1 formulates the problem, sections 3.2 and 3.3 define the posterior teacher and its process reward, and section 3.4 trains the agent on this reward.

3.1 Problem formulation

Exact posterior.

A simulator knows more than the agent trained in it. Prior work passes this privileged information to a teacher or a critic as the true state (Pinto et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019; Choudhury and Sodhi, 2025), while we use it to compute the exact posterior over what the agent cannot see. Each task has a hidden target θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta drawn from a prior p0p_{0}, a correct answer y∗​(θ)∈𝒴y^{*}(\theta)\in\mathcal{Y}, and evidence actions at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} with observations ot∼p(⋅∣θ,a1:t)o_{t}\sim p(\cdot\mid\theta,a_{1:t}). In the cups task of figure 2, θ\theta is the cup hiding the red cylinder, an evidence action lifts a cup, and an answer names a cup. The simulators of our tasks in section 4.1 enumerate Θ\Theta, and before every step tt they compute the exact posterior

bt(θ)∝p0(θ)∏s<tp(os∣θ,a1:s).b_{t}(\theta)\propto p_{0}(\theta)\textstyle\prod_{s<t}p(o_{s}\mid\theta,a_{1:s}). (1)

Since all our tasks have deterministic observations, btb_{t} is p0p_{0} restricted to the targets consistent with every observation. We write bt​(y)b_{t}(y) for the posterior probability that yy is correct, bt​(Y)b_{t}(Y) for the mass of a set Y⊆𝒴Y\subseteq\mathcal{Y}, and Bt∗={y∈𝒴:bt​(y)>0}B^{*}_{t}=\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:b_{t}(y)>0\} for the answers still allowed by the evidence. We drop the index tt when the history is clear. In figure 2(c), lifting cups 1 and 3 leaves B3∗={2,4}B^{*}_{3}=\{2,4\}.

Agent.

The agent is a vision-language model πϕ\pi_{\phi} that reasons before it acts (Wei et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2025). At step tt, it reads the task instruction and its history hth_{t} and writes a turn xt=(zt,βt,ut)∼πϕ(⋅∣ht)x_{t}=(z_{t},\beta_{t},u_{t})\sim\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid h_{t}). The history holds the past actions and observations and the last belief line of the agent. The turn consists of a reasoning ztz_{t} in the agent’s thinking block, a belief line βt\beta_{t} and an action ut∈𝒜∪𝒴u_{t}\in\mathcal{A}\cup\mathcal{Y}. The belief line names the set BtB_{t} of answers still possible in the agent’s view. It is exact if it names exactly the answers allowed by the evidence, too narrow if it rules out one of them, and too wide if it keeps an answer ruled out by the evidence. At h3h_{3} in figure 2, the line Possible: cups 2, 4 is exact, Possible: cup 4 is too narrow and the open line Possible: all is too wide. Because the history keeps no earlier reasoning, the belief line carries the agent’s belief from one turn to the next. We call dt=(βt,ut)d_{t}=(\beta_{t},u_{t}) the decision of the turn and treat ztz_{t} as a latent variable.

Objective.

The agent and a task form a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) (Kaelbling et al., 1998) whose hidden variable θ\theta stays fixed during an episode. An answer yy at step TstopT_{\text{stop}} ends the episode with the outcome reward

G=c(Tstop) 1[y=y∗(θ)],c(t)=e−λt/T,G=c(T_{\text{stop}})\,\mathbf{1}\big[y=y^{*}(\theta)\big],\qquad c(t)=e^{-\lambda t/T}, (2)

where λ\lambda is a time discount and TT is the step limit. An episode without an answer earns 00. An optimal agent decides using only btb_{t} and tt, because (bt,t)(b_{t},t) is a sufficient statistic of hth_{t} for 𝔼⁡[G]\mathbb{E}[G] (Åström, 1965). Choosing when to answer is an optimal stopping problem (Wald, 1947; Chow et al., 1971). The exact posterior lets us value every action with a lookahead on btb_{t}. It also lets us verify every belief line against Bt∗B^{*}_{t}. We want the agent to learn this stopping decision. It should keep going while it has insufficient evidence and answer once it has sufficient evidence. The action term also scores which evidence action the agent picks, but improving that choice is not the goal of this work. Sections 3.2 and 3.3 turn this action value and belief line check into a reward for each step.

3.2 The posterior teacher

The exact posterior gives two quantities at every history, and both depend only on the evidence. One is the value of every next action, and these values define the teacher policy π∗\pi^{*} that scores the action. The other is the set Bt∗B^{*}_{t} of answers still allowed by the evidence, and a variant also checks the belief line against this set.

The teacher values an answer yy by the log of its discounted chance of being right, and an evidence action aa by the expected value of the posterior ba,ob^{a,o} after its observation oo (Howard, 1966):

Q⁡(b,y)\displaystyle Q(b,y) =log⁡(c⁡(t)​ρ^​(b)​b​(y)/bmax),\displaystyle=\log\big(c(t)\,\hat{\rho}(b)\,b(y)/b_{\max}\big), (3)
Q(n)​(b,a)\displaystyle Q^{(n)}(b,a) =∑op⁡(o∣b,a)​V(n−1)​(ba,o),\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{o}p(o\mid b,a)\,V^{(n-1)}(b^{a,o}),
V(n)​(b)\displaystyle V^{(n)}(b) =maxu⁡Q(n)​(b,u),\displaystyle=\max_{u}Q^{(n)}(b,u),

where bmax=maxy⁡b⁡(y)b_{\max}=\max_{y}b(y), ρ^​(b)\hat{\rho}(b) is the measured answer accuracy of the agent, uu ranges over the answers and the evidence actions with Q(n)​(b,y)=Q⁡(b,y)Q^{(n)}(b,y)=Q(b,y), and nn is the depth of the lookahead (supplementary material). The teacher answers with probability pans=σ⁡(Δ/τ)p_{\text{ans}}=\sigma(\Delta/\tau), where σ\sigma is the logistic function and Δ\Delta the value of the best answer minus that of the best evidence action. It chooses among the answers or among the evidence actions by a Boltzmann distribution with temperature τ\tau (Haarnoja et al., 2017):

π∗​(y∣b)\displaystyle\pi^{*}(y\mid b) =pans​softmaxy⁡(Q⁡(b,⋅)/τ),\displaystyle=p_{\text{ans}}\,\operatorname{softmax}_{y}\big(Q(b,\cdot)/\tau\big), (4)
π∗​(a∣b)\displaystyle\pi^{*}(a\mid b) =(1−pans)​softmaxa⁡(Q(n)​(b,⋅)/τ).\displaystyle=(1-p_{\text{ans}})\,\operatorname{softmax}_{a}\big(Q^{(n)}(b,\cdot)/\tau\big).

The teacher depends on the agent only through ρ^\hat{\rho}, which is measured from the agent’s own answers. Where these answers are unreliable, answering has a low value and the teacher asks for more evidence. The stopping rule of the teacher thus fits the agent (supplementary material).

In figure 2(c), b3b_{3} splits evenly between cups 2 and 4. Answering now is right with probability at most 1/21/2, while lifting either cup reveals where the cylinder is and lets the agent answer correctly one step later. The teacher therefore puts almost all of π∗​(u∣b3)\pi^{*}(u\mid b_{3}) on the two lifts.

3.3 Posterior process rewards

The teacher gives each turn a reward at the history where the agent wrote it. The reward uses the exact belief bb, which the simulator can verify. The main term checks the action against bb. A second term, the belief term, directly checks the belief stated in the agent’s line:

R⁡(h,x)=log⁡π∗​(u∣b)⏟action+Sdec+η⁡(S+W)⏟stated belief,R(h,x)=\underbrace{\log\pi^{*}(u\mid b)}_{\text{action}}+\underbrace{S_{\text{dec}}+\eta\,(S+W)}_{\text{stated belief}}, (5)

where η\eta is a small weight. The action term is the action’s log probability under the teacher. The teacher acts on the exact belief bb. As a result, the action term rewards taking more steps while bb still allows several answers. Once bb no longer allows several answers, it rewards giving an answer. In this way, the action term is a belief-based reward. It uses the belief that the simulator can verify. It does not use the line written by the agent. The agent commits when the action uu is an answer. It keeps working when uu is an evidence action. Therefore, the action term rewards both the decision to commit or keep working and the choice of evidence action.

The action term penalizes the two possible mistakes very differently: answering before the evidence is sufficient receives a very low reward (−7.42-7.42 in figure 1), while taking one additional step after the evidence is sufficient incurs only the small time discount of a single step. The reward therefore primarily teaches the agent not to answer too early.

RLVB learns from the verifiable belief bb through the action term. In every turn, the agent writes its belief line right before its action. Because the update increases the likelihood of the whole turn, it trains the line together with the action. As section 4.6 shows, the agent then learns to commit or keep working as its own belief line says. This is the main idea of RLVB.

The belief term is a variant that also rewards the line itself. We train RLVB (EM) with both terms, and we train RLVB with the action term alone. We report the belief term as an ablation in section 4.4. It does not raise accuracy. The belief term reads the line as the uniform distribution bβb_{\beta} over BB, with log⁡bβ​(y)=−m\log b_{\beta}(y)=-m for an answer outside BB. It combines three scores of β\beta against bb:

S⁡(β,b)\displaystyle S(\beta;b) =∑yb⁡(y)​log⁡bβ​(y),\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{y}b(y)\log b_{\beta}(y), (6)
W⁡(β,b)\displaystyle W(\beta;b) =−m|B∖B∗|/|B|,\displaystyle=-m\,|B\setminus B^{*}|/|B|,
Sdec​(β,b)\displaystyle S_{\text{dec}}(\beta;b) =log⁡π∗​(aβ∣b),\displaystyle=\log\pi^{*}(a_{\beta}\mid b),

where aβ=arg⁡maxu​π∗​(u∣bβ)a_{\beta}=\arg\max_{u}\pi^{*}(u\mid b_{\beta}) is the teacher’s most probable action if the line were the posterior.

SS is the log score of the line (Good, 1952), but it punishes a line that is too narrow far more than one that is too wide. On its own, SS would teach the agent to hedge. We therefore score the line mainly by its implied decision. SdecS_{\text{dec}} is a proper scoring rule of the teacher’s decision problem (Grünwald and Dawid, 2004; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007), and WW charges a line that is too wide for the answers ruled out by the evidence. The small weight η\eta on S+WS+W breaks ties between lines that imply the same action. Since RR depends only on the posterior and the decision, no later observation enters it. Figure 1 gives both terms for the four turns at h3h_{3} in figure 2(c). The action term gives both lifts 00 and both answers −7.42-7.42, whatever their belief line. The belief term then ranks the exact line above the open line and the guess Possible: cup 4.

3.4 Policy update

RLVB updates the policy one step at a time (figure 2(c) and algorithm 1), and we train it in phases. In phase kk, a fixed copy πk\pi_{k} of the model plays episodes, and at every history hh of these episodes we sample NN turns xi∼πk(⋅∣h)x_{i}\sim\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid h) and score each by equation 5. The teacher’s action replaces the agent’s in these episodes with a probability that starts at 0.5 and decays from phase to phase, as in DAgger (Ross et al., 2011). On half of the training scenes, one more episode starts with random evidence actions, and the histories then also cover states rarely reached by the agent’s own actions. The update compares these NN decisions at the same history, and a decision is thus credited only against alternatives under the same evidence. Trajectory RL such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) instead credits every step of an episode with the advantage of the whole episode, and the two gradient estimates differ in exactly this respect:

trajectory:\displaystyle\text{trajectory:} ∑e∑tAe​∇ϕ​log⁡πϕ​(xe,t∣he,t),\displaystyle\textstyle\displaystyle\sum_{e}\sum_{t}A_{e}\,\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}(x_{e,t}\mid h_{e,t}), (7)
step:\displaystyle\text{step:} ∑h∑iwi​∇ϕ​log⁡πϕ​(xi∣h),\displaystyle\textstyle\displaystyle\sum_{h}\sum_{i}w_{i}\,\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}(x_{i}\mid h),

where AeA_{e} is shared by all the steps tt of episode ee, and wiw_{i} weighs turn ii against the other turns at hh.

Each phase moves the model toward the improved policy (Peters et al., 2010; Levine, 2018; Donsker and Varadhan, 1975)

qk​(x∣h)∝πk​(x∣h)​eR⁡(h,x)/α,q_{k}(x\mid h)\propto\pi_{k}(x\mid h)\,e^{R(h,x)/\alpha}, (8)

which maximizes 𝔼πR−αKL(π∥πk)\mathbb{E}_{\pi}R-\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{k}) at every history. The model moves toward qkq_{k} by gradient steps on the weighted log likelihood

ℒ(ϕ)=−∑h∑i=1Nwilogπϕ(xi∣h).\mathcal{L}(\phi)=-\textstyle\sum_{h}\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\log\pi_{\phi}(x_{i}\mid h). (9)

We use two weightings, the first for RLVB and the second for its variant RLVB (EM). RLVB uses the policy gradient (Williams, 1992). It is group relative as in GRPO, but its group is the NN turns at one history. Each turn is weighted by its reward minus the mean reward of the other turns (Ahmadian et al., 2024):

wi∝R⁡(h,xi)−1N−1​∑j≠iR⁡(h,xj).w_{i}\propto R(h,x_{i})-\tfrac{1}{N-1}\textstyle\sum_{j\neq i}R(h,x_{j}). (10)

This weight is proportional to R​(h,xi)−R¯​(h)R(h,x_{i})-\bar{R}(h) in figure 2(c). RLVB (EM) instead uses expectation maximization (EM) (Dempster et al., 1977; Abdolmaleki et al., 2018) and weights the turns by wi∝eR⁡(h,xi)/αw_{i}\propto e^{R(h,x_{i})/\alpha}, normalized over the history. These normalized weights estimate qkq_{k} itself. The two weightings are two limits of one family (supplementary material). To keep each step small, a phase ends when the KL divergence of πϕ\pi_{\phi} from πk\pi_{k} exceeds ε\varepsilon. Each phase is then one step of policy mirror descent on RR (Lan, 2023; Tomar et al., 2022). RLVB gives a turn its own reward only, because the lookahead of the teacher already values what follows. GRPO with process supervision (Shao et al., 2024) instead adds the rewards of all later steps to a step. With both weightings, a turn gets no positive weight if the teacher rejects its action, that is, if π∗​(u∣b)<π∗​(ubest∣b)/20\pi^{*}(u\mid b)<\pi^{*}(u_{\text{best}}\mid b)/20 for the teacher’s most probable action ubestu_{\text{best}}. A small length reward favors the shorter reasoning among correct turns, as in Kimi k1.5 (Kimi Team, 2025). The supplementary material gives the rules for sampling, acceptance and fitting.

4 Experiments

4.1 Benchmarks

We evaluate on three benchmarks: HiddenGames, Pro-Worlds and RoboQuest (Liu et al., 2026). In all benchmarks, the answer is hidden. The agent must take actions to collect evidence and decide when it has seen enough to answer.

HiddenGames.

It consists of seven tasks from existing agent benchmarks: MineSweeper (Wang et al., 2026a), MiniGrid KeyCorridor (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2023), FrozenLake and Sokoban (Wang et al., 2025a), and three Tabletop tasks rendered in ManiSkill3 (Tao et al., 2025). We train on these tasks and test on 756 of their games with seeds, maps and colors never seen in training.

Pro-Worlds.

To assess transfer to out-of-domain visual tasks, we introduce Pro-Worlds, a benchmark that tests how visual agents gather, retain and combine evidence before they commit to an answer. In each game, the agent sees a larger world only through a small window, moves the window to collect evidence, and must decide when it has seen enough to answer. The window shows one site of the world at a time. The agent can make at most 35 moves before it names one of eight candidates (ten in Jigsaw) as its answer. We compute the exact posterior of every game from its game engine. A teacher acting on this posterior solves every game in 14.7 moves on average. We test on 15 games (Face, Jigsaw, Kaleido, Bird, Fish, Recipe, Turtle, Balloon, Rocket, Bell, Bee, Candle, Sailboat, Barn and Lantern), with 20 plays of each.

RoboQuest.

To test transfer to tasks without an exact posterior, we use the ten mobile manipulation tasks of RoboQuest (Liu et al., 2026). They take place in simulated kitchens and require search, inspection and interactive testing, such as finding the odd parcel by weighing. We test on 50 games of each task. The supplementary material gives further details of all three benchmarks.

4.2 Experiment Setup

Models.

We train three open-source vision-language models: Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking and Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking (Bai et al., 2025), and Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026).

Baselines.

Base is the untrained model and outputs an action only. Base (w/ belief) is the same model with a belief line before the action. We consider two groups of trained baselines. The first group acts without a belief and learns from whole episodes. SFT fine-tunes the base model on the teacher’s actions in winning games. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) train on the outcome reward of each episode. PPO also learns a critic. The second group learns from a process reward. In PPO (belief + action), the model writes its belief as short claims with certainty words and then an action. PPO trains it with the outcome reward of the episode. A learned value function carries this reward back to every turn. At each turn, an LLM judge (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026)) rewards the belief by checking its claims against the newest observation and the true hidden state. Only the belief gets a per-turn reward. The decision to continue or to answer is rewarded only by the outcome of the episode. Both rewards of this baseline are based on the truth. The reward of RLVB is instead based on the evidence. The outcome reward pays a correct answer even when it was a guess. The judge rewards a true claim even when the evidence does not support it. PPO (belief + action) also samples whole episodes and learns from one outcome per episode. RLVB instead samples multiple turns at each history and rewards each of them against the exact posterior. All methods train LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022) for up to 50 updates on the same tasks. At every turn, every method receives the full history of its actions and observations but not its earlier reasoning.

Metrics.

We test the adapter after the last update of each run. Each test runs three times with different sampling seeds. We report the mean accuracy over the three runs11 1 The accuracy of RLVB varies by up to 4% across training runs. When trained three times on Qwen3.5-4B with small changes to the settings, the three runs reached 48.5 to 50.0% on HiddenGames, 28.3 to 32.1% on Pro-Worlds, and 54.0 to 56.9% on RoboQuest.. Accuracy is the share of episodes ending with the correct answer. The supplementary material lists the settings of RLVB.

4.3 Main results

Table 1 reports the accuracy of every method.

Stating a belief.

Stating a belief helps even without training. Base (w/ belief) is better than Base in eight of the nine settings. It improves over Base by 3.8% on average, and by 11.6% with Qwen3.5-4B on HiddenGames. However, stating a belief does not stop early answers. Base (w/ belief) still commits on 3 to 68% of turns where it has insufficient evidence and its own belief line names several answers (section 4.6).

Comparison with the baselines.

RLVB has the highest accuracy. RLVB or RLVB (EM) is the best method in eight of the nine columns of table 1. Both learners improve Base in every setting, by 17.1% on average with RLVB and by 10.4% with RLVB (EM). Both also outperform SFT, GRPO and PPO (action-only) in every setting. The gains transfer to the two benchmarks never seen in training, by up to 17.6% on Pro-Worlds and up to 32.8% on RoboQuest. In contrast, the outcome reward helps little. On average, GRPO (action-only) loses 1.0% and PPO (action-only) loses 5.1%. The gain comes mainly from the posterior reward, because two different learners both give large gains with it. RLVB and GRPO (action-only) use the same learner, which weights each sample against its group. With this learner, the posterior process reward outperforms the outcome reward in all nine settings, by 18.1% on average.

Judged process reward.

RLVB is also better than a judged process reward. PPO (belief + action) gains 7.9% over Base on average. RLVB does better than it in eight of the nine settings, by 9.3% on average. The only exception is RoboQuest with Qwen3.5-4B. To compare their behavior, we replay every test episode and compute the exact posterior at each turn. We report the results in table 2. Across all nine settings, RLVB produces the fewest premature answers and takes the most steps. On HiddenGames, 34.5–43.1% of answers from RLVB are premature, compared to 58.9–94.3% for PPO (belief + action) and 64.2–95.1% for Base (w/ belief). However, its belief line is not the most often exact in any of the six settings. Section 4.6 shows that this gain comes from acting on the belief line. The agent rarely commits while the line still names several answers.

4.4 Ablation

The sample set and the two terms of the reward.

Table 3 reports runs that change one setting of RLVB at a time on Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking. In every run, the agent still writes a belief line before each action and receives it at the next turn. Only the training changes. RLVB trains with the action term of equation 5.

We first reduce the sample set to 300 histories and use 200 of them. The accuracy then stays about the same on HiddenGames, at 35.3% against 36.2%, but falls from 28.7% to 23.9% on Pro-Worlds and from 61.2% to 55.5% on RoboQuest. The larger sample set therefore helps on the two benchmarks never seen in training.

Next, we keep the small sample set and add the belief term. The accuracy does not rise with this term. It stays about the same on HiddenGames, at 35.9% against 35.3%, and falls from 23.9% to 21.7% on Pro-Worlds and from 55.5% to 45.8% on RoboQuest.

Finally, we keep the belief term and remove the action term. The reward of a turn is then its belief term alone. We also turn off the acceptance rule of section 3.4, because it uses the teacher’s probability of the action. The accuracy is then the same as that of Base (w/ belief) on HiddenGames, at 24.6% against 24.5%. It is lower on Pro-Worlds, at 14.6% against 18.2%, and on RoboQuest, at 19.7% against 34.0%. The gain of RLVB therefore comes from the action term. A reward on the belief line alone does not teach the agent when to continue and when to answer.

Adding a process reward.

PPO (action-only) and PPO (belief + action) use the same learner and the same outcome reward. Only PPO (belief + action) adds a process reward from an LLM judge that scores the belief at every turn. In table 1, this process reward raises accuracy in eight of the nine settings, by 13.0% on average. The two runs also differ in the turn format, because only PPO (belief + action) states a belief. In the two base rows, the belief line alone changes accuracy by 3.8% on average. In six of the nine settings, the gap between the two runs is larger than this change. This suggests that most of the gain comes from the process reward.

4.5 Analysis

Training time.

Table 4 gives the cost of each training run. On Qwen3.5-4B with A100 GPUs, PPO (belief + action) uses 1.6×\times as many GPU-hours as RLVB (120.1 against 74.2) and also makes about 12,600 calls to an LLM judge. RLVB (EM) uses 29.7 GPU-hours, which is four times less than PPO (belief + action). RLVB is cheaper because its reward is computed from the exact posterior and needs no value network and no reward model. PPO (belief + action) instead trains a value network next to the policy and asks an LLM judge to score every belief. At this lower cost, RLVB is still more accurate than PPO (belief + action) in eight of the nine columns of table 1.

RLVB (EM) against RLVB.

The two learners both yield large gains, reaching a mean accuracy of 42.7% for RLVB and 36.0% for RLVB (EM). RLVB (EM) outperforms RLVB in one of the nine columns of table 1, while in table 2, RLVB produces fewer premature answers than RLVB (EM) across all three benchmarks. Because RLVB (EM) retains the belief term, the two rows also differ in their reward. In the rows with the belief term in table 5, where RLVB is trained with the same reward as RLVB (EM), its mean accuracy is 38.5%, compared to 36.0% for RLVB (EM). The learner of RLVB is therefore better under either reward. RLVB (EM) is the more efficient learner, because it needs only 32–44% of the GPU-hours of RLVB to reach its accuracy (table 4).

Learning signal.

Figure 3 shows why the outcome reward helps little. With GRPO, a group without a winning episode gives every episode the same reward and therefore no learning signal. After 50 updates, 18.8–53.1% of the groups are of this kind. The success of GRPO on the training batch does not rise. With the posterior reward, few groups of RLVB give no signal. Their share is about 2% for the two Qwen3-VL models and 14% for Qwen3.5-4B.

Fewer premature answers.

Because the reward of RLVB comes from the exact posterior, it penalizes a guess even when the guess is right and rewards further steps while the evidence is not enough. We pool HiddenGames, Pro-Worlds and RoboQuest. Each range below spans the three models. Before the evidence is enough, Base answers at 11 to 20% of the turns and RLVB at only 3%. PPO (belief + action) also writes a belief, but its reward checks the belief against the true answer instead of the evidence. This reward can therefore still pay a lucky guess. PPO (belief + action) gives 56 to 83% of its answers too early. In table 6, the share of premature answers falls from 76–87% for Base to 44–46% for RLVB. Section 4.6 examines where the gain comes from.

How much evidence the agents gather.

Figure 4 shows how the evidence grows with the number of steps. On HiddenGames and Pro-Worlds, it plots the exact posterior of the correct answer after each step. RoboQuest has no posterior. On RoboQuest, the figure plots the share of episodes where the feedback meets every task requirement. Each curve rises while that method’s agents still take steps. It flattens once they stop. As a result, the curves separate where the methods stop. On Pro-Worlds, the curves overlap over the first steps. This happens because every method takes steps for a while, and each step gives about the same evidence for every method. On HiddenGames, RLVB’s curve closely follows the dash-dot line of random steps. On Pro-Worlds, the curves for all methods lie above it by about the same amount. RLVB takes the most steps for all three models on all three benchmarks. Its evidence keeps growing after the other methods stop. At the end of the episodes, RLVB has more evidence than Base on all three benchmarks. On HiddenGames, the posterior of the correct answer is 59 to 64% for RLVB, compared to 22 to 37% for Base. On Pro-Worlds, it is 38 to 42% for RLVB, compared to 17 to 25% for Base. On RoboQuest, the feedback meets every task requirement in 68 to 77% of RLVB’s episodes, compared to 31 to 45% for Base (table 23). Section 4.6 shows that RLVB takes these extra steps because it does not commit while its belief line still names several answers.

The belief line and the belief reward.

For Base (w/ belief), the belief line is already exact on many turns. It is exact on 46.8 to 48.4% of turns on HiddenGames and on 75.7 to 82.4% of turns on Pro-Worlds. Yet the model often does not act on this belief. It commits on 3 to 68% of the turns where the evidence is insufficient and its own belief line still names several answers (section 4.6). We test whether rewarding the belief line fixes this problem. For this test, table 5 compares training with and without the belief term in equation 5. We replay every test episode using the exact posterior. At each turn, we count how many answers the belief line names and how many answers the evidence still allows. On HiddenGames, we look at Qwen3-VL-4B trained with the belief term and select the turns where its belief line names a single answer. The agent answers on 98% of these turns when the evidence allows only that answer, and on 95% of them when the evidence still allows several. With the belief term, the agent commits on almost every single-answer line, whether or not the evidence supports it. This matters because the evidence still allows several answers on about half of the turns where the belief line names one answer. RLVB is trained without the belief term, and it treats these two kinds of turns differently. It answers on 66% of the turns where the evidence allows only one answer, and on 32% of the turns where the evidence still allows several. The other two models show the same change. On HiddenGames, the belief term makes the belief line exact more often for the two Qwen3-VL models (57 against 41% and 70 against 46% of turns). It does not do so for Qwen3.5-4B (53 against 60%). With the belief term, the agent also answers earlier. On HiddenGames, 43.0 to 52.9% of its answers are premature, compared to 34.5 to 43.1% for RLVB, as table 2 shows. The belief term does not raise accuracy on any model. Removing the belief term helps most on RoboQuest. Without the belief term, 20.0 to 28.9% of the agent’s RoboQuest answers come before it has seen what the task requires, compared to 25.3 to 41.9% with the belief term.

With the belief term, the agent commits whenever its belief line names a single answer. With the action term alone, the agent rarely commits while the evidence is insufficient and its belief line names several answers. Removing the belief term does not remove the belief from the reward. The action term is still computed from the exact belief verified by the simulator. Therefore, RLVB’s main effect is on the decision to commit. As table 2 shows, RLVB changes the share of exact belief lines over all turns by −5.8-5.8 to +12.5+12.5% on HiddenGames and by −7.8-7.8 to −4.9-4.9% on Pro-Worlds. The rise on Qwen3.5-4B comes from fewer belief lines that cannot be read, at 1.3% of turns compared to 29.5%.

4.6 Why RLVB works

There are three possible explanations for RLVB’s gain. The trained agent could read its evidence better (RQ1), take steps that bring more evidence (RQ2), or act on what its belief line says (RQ3). In terms of metacognition, RQ1 and RQ2 look at monitoring the evidence. RQ3 looks at whether controlling the decision follows this monitoring. At every turn, the exact posterior measures how strongly the evidence gathered so far settles the answer. This lets us test each explanation.

We call each evidence-gathering action a step. We call the evidence sufficient when the exact posterior of the top answer is at least 0.95. RoboQuest has no posterior, so there the evidence is sufficient once all evidence requirements of the task are met. We define the evidence at the answer as the top answer’s posterior on the turn when the agent commits. On RoboQuest, it is the share of requirements met on that turn. A belief line is exact when it names exactly the answers that are still possible. Base is the base model without a belief line. Base (w/ belief) is the same model with a belief line. In this section, HiddenGames means its five tasks with an answer, and RoboQuest means its eight tasks with countable requirements. The accuracies therefore differ from those in table 1. Appendix K gives details of these measures and further tests.

The evidence at the answer.

Figure 5 groups each method’s episodes by the evidence at the answer. HiddenGames and Pro-Worlds use four levels because the posterior takes only a few values there. RoboQuest uses six levels. Across all methods, answers given with sufficient evidence are correct in 66 to 92% of cases, against 0 to 13% at the lowest level. The base model gives most of its answers at low evidence levels. It answers with a posterior below 40% in 79% of its HiddenGames episodes and 96% of its Pro-Worlds episodes. In contrast, RLVB commits at much higher evidence levels. It answers with sufficient evidence in 51% of HiddenGames episodes, 12% on Pro-Worlds and 74% on RoboQuest, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for Base and 20%, 3% and 57% for PPO (belief + action). As a result, the mean evidence at the answer is higher for RLVB than for Base by 47.4% in HiddenGames (95% interval from 45.4 to 49.4%), 20.6% on Pro-Worlds (from 19.4 to 21.8%), and 34.8% on RoboQuest (from 32.5 to 37.0%). Across individual models, this difference is between 18 and 51%, as figure 10 shows.

Where the gain comes from.

A method can improve its accuracy in two ways. First, it can answer at higher levels of evidence by taking more steps before it commits. Second, it can answer more accurately at the same level of evidence, for example by reading its observations better. To measure both effects, we write a method’s accuracy as a sum over evidence levels ee. Each term multiplies the share of episodes answered at that level, f⁡(e)f(e), by the accuracy of the answers at that level, a⁡(e)a(e). We count episodes with no answer as wrong. The gain of a method MM over Base BB then splits exactly into two parts,

AccM−AccB=∑e(fM​(e)−fB​(e))​a¯​(e)⏟more evidence+∑e(aM​(e)−aB​(e))​f¯​(e)⏟same evidence,\mathrm{Acc}_{M}-\mathrm{Acc}_{B}=\underbrace{\sum_{e}\bigl(f_{M}(e)-f_{B}(e)\bigr)\,\bar{a}(e)}_{\text{more evidence}}+\underbrace{\sum_{e}\bigl(a_{M}(e)-a_{B}(e)\bigr)\,\bar{f}(e)}_{\text{same evidence}}, (11)

where a¯​(e)\bar{a}(e) and f¯​(e)\bar{f}(e) are the two methods’ means at level ee. Figure 5(d) to figure 5(f) show these two parts for RLVB. RLVB is more accurate because a larger share of its answers come at high levels of evidence, where every method’s answers are often correct. At the same level of evidence, RLVB’s answers are no more accurate than Base’s. In HiddenGames, the 18.1% gain splits into +26.7+26.7% from more evidence and −8.5-8.5% at the same evidence. On Pro-Worlds, the two parts are +15.8+15.8 and −2.8-2.8%. On RoboQuest, they are +31.8+31.8 and +0.3+0.3%. In HiddenGames, the second part is negative because RLVB misreads more of its sufficient evidence, as RQ1 shows. Table 21 reports both parts for each model and for PPO (belief + action). Answers with sufficient evidence are also correct much more often than other answers in the same test game. RLVB gives a correct answer with sufficient evidence in 33.3% of HiddenGames episodes, 8.7% of Pro-Worlds episodes, and 66.6% of RoboQuest episodes. Base does so in 7.5%, 0.3%, and 31.7% of episodes, as table 22 shows.

RQ1: Does RLVB read its evidence better?

We measure what the agent reads from its evidence through its belief line. Because RLVB’s update raises the likelihood of the entire turn, this belief line is trained alongside the actions even though the reward scores only the action. Over all turns, RLVB’s belief line is not consistently more accurate than the belief line of Base (w/ belief). Table 7 reports the share of turns where the belief line is exact. We count every turn, and we count a line that cannot be read as not exact. In HiddenGames, RLVB’s belief line is exact more often on Qwen3.5-4B, at 60.3% against 47.8%, but it is exact less often on the two Qwen3-VL models. On Pro-Worlds, it is exact less often on all three models, by 4.9 to 7.8%. On RoboQuest, it is exact more often on the two Qwen3-VL models, by 5.9 and 12.2%, and about as often on Qwen3.5-4B. Within HiddenGames, it is exact more often on the Tabletop tasks for every model, by 1.6 to 11.9%, as table 29 shows.

At the same states, RLVB’s belief line is more cautious. Table 8 compares the agents on states that all of them reach while several answers remain. On these states, RLVB’s belief line names a single answer less often than Base’s belief line in all nine settings. The 95% interval of the difference excludes zero in eight of those settings. RLVB’s belief line is also exact more often in all nine settings. Figure 6(a) shows the same pattern after every number of steps on the Tabletop tasks. Over all turns, this caution does not make the belief line more exact for two reasons. First, RLVB spends many turns at later states that Base rarely reaches. Second, its belief line more often still names several answers after the evidence has become sufficient, as table 29 shows.

Once the belief line narrows to a single answer, this answer is often wrong. At the last turn of an episode that ends with an answer, RLVB’s belief line names a single answer in 83% of the Tabletop episodes. That answer is correct in 57% of those cases, or in 70% when the evidence is sufficient, as table 10 shows. After the same number of steps, the two agents’ single answers are correct about equally often. With sufficient evidence, these answers are correct in 93–100% of cases after one step for both agents. After two steps, they are correct in 68–73% of cases for RLVB and 70–76% for Base, as figure 6(b) shows. RLVB takes more steps. On the two Qwen3-VL models, its single answers are correct less often as steps add up. After four or more steps, they are correct in 36–39% of cases. Base almost never reaches that many steps. When RLVB gives a wrong answer with sufficient evidence on the Tabletop tasks, its belief line excludes the true answer in 85–97% of cases, as table 30 shows.

RQ2: Does RLVB judge what further steps can bring?

If RLVB had learned to anticipate upcoming evidence, it would choose steps that add more evidence than those of Base and recognize when its own steps stop adding evidence. We measure the value of a step by how much it raises the exact posterior of the correct answer, or by the share of requirements met on RoboQuest. By this measure, steps from RLVB add about as much evidence as those from Base. From the states reached by Base, PPO (belief + action), and RLVB, the first step raises the posterior by 15.6, 14.9, and 14.8% in HiddenGames and by 1.5, 1.9, and 1.5% on Pro-Worlds, while meeting 19.1, 19.3, and 19.8% of the requirements on RoboQuest, as appendix K shows. Later steps have similar value across every window of steps from the start of the game, as figure 7 shows. Across states reached by both Base and RLVB, about 20% of each agent’s actions meet one more requirement on RoboQuest, and 4–6% of their moves add evidence on Pro-Worlds, as table 9 shows. Only in MiniGrid and MineSweeper does the first step of RLVB add less evidence, raising the posterior by 0.14%, against 1.24% for Base.

RLVB also does not choose better actions. Measured against the actions ranked best by the posterior teacher, RLVB and Base choose a best action about equally often, in 40 versus 37% of HiddenGames states and 53 versus 52% of Pro-Worlds states. A better belief line does not lead to better steps either. From the same state and with an exact belief line, a step from RLVB raises the posterior of the correct answer by 0.9% more than a step from Base (w/ belief) on the Tabletop tasks, where a step adds about 30%, and by 0.02% less on Pro-Worlds, where a step adds about 0.9%. The 95% intervals for both differences include zero. The same holds when the posterior teacher continues playing to the end after each step. With an exact belief line, a step from RLVB leaves the teacher with as many remaining steps as one from Base (w/ belief) on Pro-Worlds and in the Tabletop tasks, and 0.53 more in MiniGrid and MineSweeper, as appendix K shows.

RLVB also does not recognize when its own steps stop adding evidence. In MineSweeper, the posterior teacher reaches sufficient evidence in 83% of scenes, as table 32 shows. RLVB’s steps rarely reach sufficient evidence, and the agent answers in only 3 to 16% of episodes. On Qwen3-VL-4B, 44 of its 81 MineSweeper episodes without an answer add no evidence across their last ten turns, as table 37 shows.

Why the steps do not improve.

Three things explain this result. First, RLVB gains the most on the Tabletop tasks. On those tasks, every step that tests a new object splits the possible answers in the same way, as appendix D shows. The choice of step does not matter on these tasks. Second, on MiniGrid and MineSweeper, the reward hardly separates a step without evidence from the best step. That kind of step only delays the teacher’s best plan by one turn. As a result, its score is lower than the best step’s score by about one time discount. This discount is 0.2 nats, or 0.5 nats in MineSweeper. An early answer scores several nats lower, for example −7.42-7.42 in figure 1. Because of this, the reward mostly teaches when to answer. Third, Pro-Worlds and RoboQuest never appear in training. Better steps on those tasks would have to carry over from the training tasks. A test on Qwen3.5-4B supports these points. With the three rules in section C.4, the teacher rejects steps without evidence. On the HiddenGames tasks with an answer, the share of steps that add evidence then rises from 21.2 to 28.0%. On Pro-Worlds, this share changes from 5.1 to 5.0%. On RoboQuest, it changes from 21.3 to 21.9%. Accuracy changes by −0.2-0.2 to +2.9+2.9%.

RQ3: Does RLVB act on its belief line?

The base model often acts against its own belief line. Over all turns where the belief line names several answers, Base (w/ belief) commits at 3.2 to 69.1% of these turns, while RLVB commits at 0.1 to 10.0%. On RoboQuest, Base (w/ belief) commits at 3.8 to 8.7% of these turns, while RLVB commits at 1.9 to 2.6%, as figure 8(a) shows. As a result, many of the base model’s answers go against its own belief line. When the base model answers, its belief line still names several answers in 23 to 59% of its Tabletop answers, 22 to 40% in MiniGrid and MineSweeper, 57 to 91% on Pro-Worlds, and 27 to 46% on RoboQuest. For RLVB, these shares are 6 to 30%, 1 to 29%, 0.3 to 3.3%, and 20 to 24%, as figure 8(b) shows. On Pro-Worlds, RLVB gives most of its other answers with such a line after all 35 moves are used. When the evidence is also insufficient, RLVB commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of these turns, against 3.2 to 67.9% for Base (w/ belief). In all nine settings, the 95% intervals do not overlap, as table 25 shows. From the same states with insufficient evidence, Base commits in 30–49% of cases on RoboQuest, against 7–13% for RLVB. On the Tabletop tasks, Base commits in 45–87% of cases, against 5–12% for RLVB, as table 9 shows. Instead of committing, RLVB keeps working. It takes 2.6 to 3.1 steps on the Tabletop tasks, which is close to the posterior teacher’s 2.5 steps. Base takes 0.1 to 0.8 steps.

Like Base, RLVB gives the answer that its belief line names when it commits after a single-answer line. Both agents give the named answer in at least 97% of these commits in all nine settings, and in at least 96% on RoboQuest, as figure 8 shows. RLVB rarely commits when the evidence is insufficient and its belief line names several answers. Because of this, it answers with a single-answer belief line far more often than Base. This happens in 83 against 63% of answered Tabletop episodes, 40 against 20% on Pro-Worlds, and 79 against 66% on RoboQuest, as table 10 shows. To separate acting on the belief line from forming it, we combine the share of turns where one agent’s belief line names a single answer, taken from table 29, with the other agent’s commit rates for each kind of line, taken from table 25. We average the result over both orders. Acting on the belief line accounts for 53 to 83% of the drop in early commits on the Tabletop tasks, nearly all of it on Pro-Worlds, and about four fifths on RoboQuest. The rest comes from the belief line naming a single answer too early less often.

RLVB acts on its belief line almost entirely through its first single-answer line. Figure 9 compares its accuracy with the accuracy it would reach by committing to that line’s answer. The two accuracies differ by at most 2.3% in all nine settings. When RLVB keeps working after such a line, it most often gives the same answer later. Changes from a wrong answer to a right answer happen about as often as changes from a right answer to a wrong answer. Its extra step most often tests the named answer. On Qwen3-VL-4B, it lifts the named cup in 46 of 48 such steps on cups. On lamps, it presses the last button in 177 of 198 such steps, and the belief line has already inferred that button’s lamp. After this step, its belief line names the same answer in 74% of cases, and it commits on the next turn in 88%. This check rarely corrects a wrong belief line because the next line names the same wrong answer in 66% of cases. The check also depends little on the evidence. Pooled over the three models on the Tabletop tasks, RLVB commits at 78.5% of single-answer turns with insufficient evidence and at 78.6% with sufficient evidence. Because RLVB gives the answer that its belief line names, errors in the belief line become wrong answers. This produces the negative second part of equation 11 in HiddenGames.

A likely reason for this behavior lies in the reward. The reward never reads the belief line, and it scores every action against the exact posterior. A commit gets a low reward when the evidence leaves several answers open, even if the guess happens to be correct. In contrast, an outcome reward gives a lucky guess the full reward. At these states, the belief line usually names several answers. The update raises the likelihood of the whole turn, including the line. As a result, the agent learns to keep working when its own line names several answers. Taking one more step after the evidence is sufficient costs only that step’s small time discount in the action term, as section 3.3 describes. This makes the extra check cheap. Adding a reward on the belief line itself does not raise accuracy, as table 5 shows.

The on-policy variant of RLVB doubts its belief line more and keeps exploring. On Qwen3-VL-4B, after it takes a step while its belief line names a single answer, its next line keeps that answer in 61% of cases, against 74% for RLVB. It commits on the next turn in 71%, against 88%. Of these steps, 20% are rejected as invalid, against 5%. On the Tabletop tasks, its belief line still names several answers on 62% of turns with sufficient evidence, against 46% for RLVB. It commits at only 9% of these turns, against 37% for RLVB. It ends half of its HiddenGames episodes without an answer, against 18% for RLVB. It is less accurate than RLVB on all three benchmarks, as appendix L shows.

A check in the harness.

Such a check cannot replace an agent that acts on its own belief. Our harness does not accept an episode’s first answer. It asks the agent once to check whether its evidence identifies the answer. The agent can then repeat its answer, change it, or keep working. This check raises Base’s accuracy by 6.1 to 11.3% on RoboQuest. On HiddenGames and Pro-Worlds, it changes accuracy by at most 1.9%, as table 36 shows. On the Tabletop tasks, Base keeps working after the check in only 2 to 17% of the checked episodes, as appendix K shows. Otherwise, it repeats its answer. In these tasks, Base (w/ belief) has a belief line that already names a single answer in 38 to 72% of its early commits. Because the harness does not read the observations, it cannot tell the agent when its evidence is sufficient. RLVB writes its belief line from its own observations, and that line guides most of its decisions to commit.

Limits.

An agent that keeps working gains only where its steps bring evidence. Among the HiddenGames tasks, RLVB gains most on the Tabletop tasks, where every valid step adds evidence, with 51% on lamps and 35% on cups, as appendix F shows. On RoboQuest, where about one action in five meets a requirement, the gain on the three models is 14 to 33%, and on Pro-Worlds, where about one move in twenty adds evidence, the gain is 12 to 15%. In MiniGrid and MineSweeper, a step raises the posterior of the correct answer by about 1% or less, and RLVB shows no gain on these tasks. As RQ2 shows, RLVB has not learned to commit to its best answer in MineSweeper when its steps stop adding evidence or when no step remains. Across the three models, RLVB ends 19% of its HiddenGames episodes without an answer, compared with 7% for Base, almost all of them in MineSweeper.

5 Limitations

RLVB needs a task with known rules. The environment can compute the exact posterior only when it knows the prior over the hidden answer and the likelihood of each observation. Many puzzles, games, and simulated household tasks meet this condition. For tasks with unknown or open-ended rules, the posterior must be estimated. Very large action spaces need a shallower or sampled lookahead. The cost of the teacher’s lookahead grows with the number of actions and observations. Finally, a belief line names a set of possible answers. This set states the posterior exactly only when every possible answer is equally likely. The belief line cannot express finer degrees of certainty. With training, wrong answers given with enough evidence also rise from 2–4% to 10–15% of the episodes, mostly in the Tabletop tasks (tables 6 and 30). On these tasks, the agent misreads observations that already settle the answer. It then gives the wrong answer that its belief line names (section 4.6). The action term also scores which step the agent takes, but the trained agent does not choose more informative steps. On Pro-Worlds, a step by the posterior teacher raises the posterior by 5.9%, compared to 0.7 to 1.3% for a step by any method. The trained agents also stay far below the posterior teacher (for example 32.4% against 100% on Pro-Worlds). The agents have not yet learned much of what the exact posterior allows.

6 Conclusion

We showed that a simulator can compute the exact posterior of an evidence-seeking task from its privileged information. This posterior gives a process reward at every turn. The posterior scores the agent’s choice between taking more steps and answering. It can also score the agent’s stated belief. RLVB learns from this reward with a policy gradient, and RLVB (EM) learns from it with EM. Across three vision-language models and three benchmarks, both RLVB learners improve the base model in every setting. With the same learner, the posterior process reward beats the outcome reward by 18.1% on average. On each of the three benchmarks, RLVB also beats a process reward from an LLM judge on average. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12%, and 74% of episodes, compared to 8%, 0.4%, and 36% for the base model. It does this by acting on its own belief. With the same belief line, it commits on only 0.1 to 2.2% of turns with insufficient evidence where this line still names several answers, compared to 3 to 68% for the base model. Across all turns, its belief line is not consistently more exact than the base model’s. Each of its steps adds about as much evidence as a step from the base model. A check in the harness does not raise the base model’s accuracy on HiddenGames and Pro-Worlds because the harness cannot read the observations. We expect a better reading of the evidence to carry into the answers when an agent acts on its belief. RLVB’s steps are not yet more informative than the base model’s. An agent with sufficient evidence can still misread its observations. We want to extend RLVB to tasks where the posterior must be learned, to improve the choice of the next step, and to train the agent to read its observations correctly once its evidence is sufficient.
