Supplementary Material

 

Appendix A The posterior teacher in detail

This section describes the posterior teacher of section 3.2 in detail.

Boundary values.

In equation 3, V(0)​(b)=log⁡c⁡(t)+log⁡ρ^+​(b)V^{(0)}(b)=\log c(t)+\log\hat{\rho}^{+}(b). Here ρ^+\hat{\rho}^{+} is an upper confidence bound on ρ^\hat{\rho} that adds one standard deviation, as given in equation 13. This bound is high for belief classes with few measured answers. The lookahead thus gives a high value to evidence that leads to these classes. The time of ba,ob^{a,o} is t+1t+1. A belief at the step limit t=Tt=T and a belief that identifies the answer both have the value log⁡c​(t)+log⁡ρ^​(b)\log c(t)+\log\hat{\rho}(b). For an answer with b⁡(y)=0b(y)=0, we floor the accuracy at 10−910^{-9}. Such an answer has the value log⁡c⁡(t)+log⁡10−9\log c(t)+\log 10^{-9}. An outcome that ends the episode without an answer, such as a revealed mine, has the value of knowing nothing, log⁡c⁡(t)+log⁡(1/|Θ|)\log c(t)+\log(1/|\Theta|). A lookahead of depth 2 evaluates every pair of evidence actions with their observations. Its cost thus grows as (|𝒜|​|𝒪|)2(|\mathcal{A}|\,|\mathcal{O}|)^{2} Bayes updates per history.

Task lookaheads.

We use equation 3 with depth 2 for the Tabletop tasks. The other tasks have many evidence actions. Each of them computes the same kind of value, log⁡c⁡(t)+log⁡ρ^\log c(t)+\log\hat{\rho}, with its own lookahead. MiniGrid, FrozenLake and Sokoban value each move by the best view reached on a shortest plan starting with this move. MineSweeper values each reveal by the posterior after it. The cost above holds for the depth-2 recursion only.

Why the logarithm.

The average of log⁡ρ^\log\hat{\rho} counts progress at every step. Each halving of the possible answers adds log⁡2\log 2, whether it comes early or late. For a uniform posterior, this average is the expected information gain on the answer. When the answers are many, the average of ρ^\hat{\rho} itself stays close to 0 until the answer is almost decided. For example, on a 6×66\times 6 MineSweeper board with 6 mines and 1,947,792 mine sets, the average of ρ^\hat{\rho} cannot rank the actions. It also gives almost no cost to a risk that ends the episode.

Answer accuracy.

ρ^​(b)\hat{\rho}(b) is the measured answer accuracy of the agent:

ρ^​(b)\displaystyle\hat{\rho}(b) =bmaxφ^κ⁡(b),ry=b⁡(y)bmax,\displaystyle=b_{\max}\,\hat{\varphi}_{\kappa(b)},\qquad r_{y}=\frac{b(y)}{b_{\max}}, (12)
φ^κ\displaystyle\hat{\varphi}_{\kappa} =4+∑ω∈Ωκ1n¯​∑y∈ωry4+∑ω∈Ωκnωn¯.\displaystyle=\frac{4+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{\kappa}}\frac{1}{\bar{n}}\sum_{y\in\omega}r_{y}}{4+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{\kappa}}\frac{n_{\omega}}{\bar{n}}}.

κ⁡(b)\kappa(b) is the belief class. It is the number of answers still possible, capped at 4. φ^κ\hat{\varphi}_{\kappa} is the mean of rr over the agent’s answers in class κ\kappa, with a prior mean of 1 and 4 pseudo-counts. φ^=1\hat{\varphi}=1 when the agent always names the most probable answer. Each update gives one measurement for each cell ω=(scene,belief class)\omega=(\text{scene},\text{belief class}). This measurement is the mean of rr over all of the agent’s answers in ω\omega. This mean replaces a single sample by its conditional mean given the cell. As in the Rao–Blackwell theorem (Rao, 1945; Blackwell, 1947), it thus has a smaller variance than one sample. nωn_{\omega} is the number of answers in ω\omega. n¯\bar{n} is the mean of nωn_{\omega} over all cells measured in the same update as ω\omega. Ωκ\Omega_{\kappa} is the set of cells of class κ\kappa measured so far over all updates. Each ryr_{y} is taken at the belief where the agent gave the answer yy. Episodes starting with random evidence actions keep each belief class measured.

The estimate φ^κ\hat{\varphi}_{\kappa} is the mean of a Beta posterior with parameters Aκ=4+∑ω∈Ωκ1n¯​∑y∈ωryA_{\kappa}=4+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{\kappa}}\frac{1}{\bar{n}}\sum_{y\in\omega}r_{y} and Aκ+Dκ=4+∑ω∈Ωκnωn¯A_{\kappa}+D_{\kappa}=4+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{\kappa}}\frac{n_{\omega}}{\bar{n}}. The upper confidence bound adds one standard deviation of this posterior:

ρ^+​(b)\displaystyle\hat{\rho}^{+}(b) =min{1,bmax(φ^κ+sdκ)},κ=κ(b),\displaystyle=\min\big\{1,\ b_{\max}\,(\hat{\varphi}_{\kappa}+\mathrm{sd}_{\kappa})\big\},\quad\kappa=\kappa(b), (13)
sdκ\displaystyle\mathrm{sd}_{\kappa} =Aκ​Dκ(Aκ+Dκ)2​(Aκ+Dκ+1).\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{A_{\kappa}\,D_{\kappa}}{(A_{\kappa}+D_{\kappa})^{2}\,(A_{\kappa}+D_{\kappa}+1)}}.

Teacher policy.

In equation 4, we normalize the step level over the groups 𝒢⁡(b)\mathcal{G}(b) of evidence actions with equal values Q(2)​(b,⋅)Q^{(2)}(b,\cdot). Each action in a group gets the full probability of its group. The step level of π∗\pi^{*} is thus a distribution over groups. If bb identifies the answer, pans=1p_{\text{ans}}=1. An answer outside the support of bb has accuracy 0. It thus gets the floor value log⁡c⁡(t)+log⁡10−9\log c(t)+\log 10^{-9}. An action that cannot be executed in the environment uses up the turn. It has the value of an answer one step later, log⁡c⁡(t+1)+log⁡ρ^​(b)\log c(t+1)+\log\hat{\rho}(b). The log-probability has the floor −200-200. π∗\pi^{*} depends on the agent only through ρ^\hat{\rho}. Where the agent’s answers are not reliable, Q⁡(b,y)Q(b,y) is low and π∗\pi^{*} asks for more evidence. The stopping rule of the teacher thus fits the agent.

Proposition 1 (What the teacher optimizes).

Suppose the lookahead reaches the step limit and ρ^\hat{\rho} is the true answer accuracy of the agent. Then, as τ→0\tau\to 0, the best action of π∗\pi^{*} maximizes 𝔼⁡[log⁡(c⁡(Tstop)​ρ^​(bTstop))]\mathbb{E}\big[\log\big(c(T_{\text{stop}})\,\hat{\rho}(b_{T_{\text{stop}}})\big)\big].

Proof sketch.

We have maxy⁡Q⁡(b,y)=log⁡c⁡(t)+log⁡ρ^​(b)\max_{y}Q(b,y)=\log c(t)+\log\hat{\rho}(b). With depth n≥T−tn\geq T-t, equation 3 is therefore the Bellman recursion of the stopping problem with the reward log⁡c​(t)+log⁡ρ^​(b)\log c(t)+\log\hat{\rho}(b) at the stop. By backward induction on the steps left, V(n)V^{(n)} is its optimal value. As τ→0\tau\to 0, π∗\pi^{*} puts all its mass on the maximizers of the values. ∎

The best action of π∗\pi^{*} therefore maximizes the expected log of the discounted answer accuracy. The proposition holds for the recursion of equation 3. The task lookaheads above approximate this recursion. With depth 2, Q(2)Q^{(2)} approximates this optimum. This criterion differs from the expected return. It prefers steady progress to a gamble that can lose all the evidence. If ρ^\hat{\rho} is the true accuracy, 𝔼⁡[G]=𝔼⁡[c⁡(Tstop)​ρ^​(bTstop)]\mathbb{E}[G]=\mathbb{E}\big[c(T_{\text{stop}})\,\hat{\rho}(b_{T_{\text{stop}}})\big]. By Jensen’s inequality, the teacher’s criterion is then a lower bound on log⁡𝔼⁡[G]\log\mathbb{E}[G]. The gap between the two makes the teacher averse to risk.

Appendix B The process reward in detail

This section describes the process reward in equation 5 in detail. The action term is the reward for RLVB. It scores the action against the teacher. The teacher acts on the exact belief bb, and the simulator can verify this belief. The belief term is a variant that also scores the stated belief line against bb. We use it in RLVB (EM) and in the ablation in section 4.4.

Action term.

The action term scores the agent’s action against the teacher policy π∗\pi^{*}. Inside one level of equation 4,

log⁡π∗​(u∣b)\displaystyle\log\pi^{*}(u\mid b) =Q¯​(b,u)τ+νℒ​(b),\displaystyle=\frac{\bar{Q}(b,u)}{\tau}+\nu_{\mathcal{L}}(b), (14)
νℒ​(b)\displaystyle\nu_{\mathcal{L}}(b) =logPℒ(b)−log∑u′∈ℒeQ¯​(b,u′)/τ,\displaystyle=\log P_{\mathcal{L}}(b)-\log\textstyle\sum_{u^{\prime}\in\mathcal{L}}e^{\bar{Q}(b,u^{\prime})/\tau},

where Q¯​(b,u)=Q​(b,y)\bar{Q}(b,u)=Q(b,y) for an answer u=yu=y, and Q¯​(b,u)=Q(2)​(b,a)\bar{Q}(b,u)=Q^{(2)}(b,a) for an evidence action u=au=a. The level ℒ\mathcal{L} of uu is “answer” or “step”. We set Panswer=pansP_{\text{answer}}=p_{\text{ans}} and Pstep=1−pansP_{\text{step}}=1-p_{\text{ans}}. For the step level, the sum runs over the groups 𝒢⁡(b)\mathcal{G}(b). Because νℒ​(b)\nu_{\mathcal{L}}(b) depends only on bb and on ℒ\mathcal{L}, the action term is a soft advantage of the lookahead values in units of τ\tau. An action whose value is one nat below the best costs 1/τ1/\tau nats. In the belief term, a line that leaves out all of the posterior mass costs mm nats in SS.

Belief language.

The belief language is the set of lines Possible: v1,…,vnv_{1},\ldots,v_{n} with distinct values vi∈Θv_{i}\in\Theta, plus the open line Possible: all, which rules out nothing. We read a line in the language exactly as its set B⊆ΘB\subseteq\Theta, and the open line as B=ΘB=\Theta. Any other text is outside the language and receives the floor of every term. The open line is thus the safe statement. A set states only the support of btb_{t}. It states btb_{t} itself only when btb_{t} is flat on its support, as when each observation is either possible or impossible under each target. The last belief line in the prompt is the agent’s own earlier estimate. In the variant with the belief term, the teacher scores each new line against btb_{t}, which comes only from the evidence. A line that copies an earlier mistake thus scores low.

Properties of the log score SS.

The stated distribution b^β\hat{b}_{\beta} is uniform on BB with the log-probability floor −m-m outside BB. Then S⁡(β,b)=𝔼θ∼b​[log⁡b^β​(θ)]=−b⁡(B)​log|B|−m⁡(1−b⁡(B))S(\beta;b)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim b}[\log\hat{b}_{\beta}(\theta)]=-b(B)\log|B|-m\,(1-b(B)).

  • •

    The log score is proper (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). Among normalized distributions, none gets a higher expected score under bb than bb itself. Because b^β\hat{b}_{\beta} is not normalized and names only a set, the property holds in the two forms below.

  • •

    When bb is flat on its support and m>1+log⁡|Θ|m>1+\log|\Theta|, the exact line β∗\beta^{*} gets the highest score.

  • •

    When bb is not flat, the best set can leave out targets of small mass. Adding a target of mass δ\delta to BB raises SS only when δ⁡(m−log⁡(|B|+1))>b⁡(B)​log⁡((|B|+1)/|B|)\delta\,\big(m-\log(|B|+1)\big)>b(B)\,\log\big((|B|+1)/|B|\big). This holds when δ\delta is above about 1/(m​|B|)1/(m|B|).

The decision score SdecS_{\text{dec}}.

Let b~β\tilde{b}_{\beta} be the belief stated by the line. It holds the targets that agree with the line. Outside MineSweeper, it also holds the targets already excluded by the evidence. Let aβa_{\beta} be the teacher’s action when b~β\tilde{b}_{\beta} is its posterior. Then Sdec​(β,b)=log⁡π∗​(aβ∣b)S_{\text{dec}}(\beta;b)=\log\pi^{*}(a_{\beta}\mid b), averaged over aβa_{\beta} when the teacher’s best actions tie. Every decision problem has its own proper scoring rule, the value of the act implied by a belief (Grünwald and Dawid, 2004; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). SdecS_{\text{dec}} is this rule for the teacher’s problem. The exact line implies the teacher’s own action and receives the highest score. SdecS_{\text{dec}} is proper but not strictly proper, because lines that imply the same act tie. The sum of a strictly proper and a proper score is strictly proper. Adding η​S\eta\,S with any η>0\eta>0 thus keeps the exact line the unique best line. If the task cannot read a line as a belief, the line receives the floor −200-200.

The mirror term WW.

W(β;b)=−m|B∖B∗|/|B|W(\beta;b)=-m\,|B\setminus B^{*}|/|B| is −m-m times the line’s probability outside the support B∗B^{*} of bb, with the line read as uniform on its options. Each task maps the line to BB and the posterior to B∗B^{*} with its own parser. WW mirrors the miss term −m⁡(1−b⁡(B))-m\,(1-b(B)) of SS. A line two times too wide pays about m/2m/2, as does a line that leaves out half of the posterior. Because W=0W=0 for the exact line and for every line inside it, the exact line keeps its score and the term needs no new constant. Under S+WS+W, the best line under the agent’s own uncertainty keeps an option when the option is more likely possible than not.

An example with three lines.

Table 11 gives the log-score part of the belief term for three lines.

Likelihood view.

Every term of RR is a log-probability or a non-positive score, and hence R≤0R\leq 0. With α=1\alpha=1, eRe^{R} lies in (0,1](0,1] and acts as the likelihood of the decision under the teacher. This view holds for RR without the length reward, because that reward adds C​ℓi≤C/2C\ell_{i}\leq C/2 to the weights. RR does not depend on the reasoning zz. The reasoning gets credit only through its effect on the probability of the decisions.

Appendix C The two learners in detail

Both learners of RLVB use the sampled turns, rewards, phases and step limit described in section C.1. Table 20 gives the settings of each reported run. They differ only in how they weight the sampled turns. Section C.2 describes EM, and section C.3 describes the policy gradient. Section C.5 shows that their weights are two limits of one family.

C.1 Shared by both learners

Proposition 2 (Improved policy).

For each history hh,

𝔼πR−αKL(π∥πk)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi}R-\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{k}) =αlogZk(h)−αKL(π∥qk),\displaystyle=\alpha\log Z_{k}(h)-\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,q_{k}), (15)
Zk​(h)\displaystyle Z_{k}(h) =𝔼x∼πk​[eR⁡(h,x)/α],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\pi_{k}}\big[e^{R(h,x)/\alpha}\big],

with qkq_{k} as in equation 8. Thus qkq_{k} is the unique maximizer of 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k}.

Proof.

This is the Gibbs variational principle (Donsker and Varadhan, 1975). Write π\pi for π(⋅∣h)\pi(\cdot\mid h). Then 𝔼πR−αKL(π∥πk)=−α𝔼πlogππk​eR/α=−α𝔼πlogπqk​Zk\mathbb{E}_{\pi}R-\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{k})=-\alpha\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\log\frac{\pi}{\pi_{k}e^{R/\alpha}}=-\alpha\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\log\frac{\pi}{q_{k}Z_{k}}, which is the right side. The last KL is zero only at π=qk\pi=q_{k}. ∎

Accepted actions.

The self-normalized weights show only the order of the samples and do not change when the same constant is added to every RR. We therefore accept a turn only when π∗​(u∣b)≥π∗​(ubest∣b)/20\pi^{*}(u\mid b)\geq\pi^{*}(u_{\text{best}}\mid b)/20, where ubestu_{\text{best}} is the action of highest probability under π∗\pi^{*}. Only accepted turns get weight. A turn with a rejected action gets weight 0 whatever its belief line. In the Bayes view, its likelihood is 0. With the belief term, the floor of the line score could otherwise give the weight to a rejected action. This could happen when every line leaves out part of the posterior. Formally, the E-step uses the score R~​(h,x)=R​(h,x)\tilde{R}(h,x)=R(h,x) for an accepted turn and R~​(h,x)=−∞\tilde{R}(h,x)=-\infty otherwise. Proposition 2, the Bayes view and equation 19 then hold with R~\tilde{R} in place of RR at every history with an accepted turn.

Covered histories.

With the action term alone, a history is covered when one of its turns has an accepted action. With the belief term, that turn must also have a belief line within 2 nats of the exact line. If no turn of the first round covers the history, the trainer samples one more round of NN turns, with 2​K2K reasonings in all. In either case, it then fits the history with its accepted turns. With the belief term, the two thresholds have two roles. The loose threshold of 2 nats decides whether to sample more. The tight threshold of 0.1 nats in the M-step decides whether a line is a target.

Histories without a target.

A history has no positive target when it has no accepted turn. With the belief term, it also has no positive target when none of its accepted turns names any of the posterior mass. Such a history gets no weight in the M-step.

Length reward.

Within one history, let |zi||z_{i}| be the number of reasoning tokens of turn ii and si=12−(|zi|−minj⁡|zj|)/(maxj⁡|zj|−minj⁡|zj|)s_{i}=\tfrac{1}{2}-(|z_{i}|-\min_{j}|z_{j}|)/(\max_{j}|z_{j}|-\min_{j}|z_{j}|), as in Kimi k1.5 (Kimi Team, 2025). A turn is correct when its action is accepted. With the belief term, its line must also be within 2 nats of the exact line. A correct turn gets ℓi=si\ell_{i}=s_{i}. Shorter correct reasoning thus gets more weight. An incorrect turn gets ℓi=min⁡(0,si)\ell_{i}=\min(0,s_{i}). A short incorrect turn thus gets no bonus, and a long one gets a penalty. All ℓi=0\ell_{i}=0 when every reasoning has the same length. From the first phase, the E-step weights add C​ℓiC\,\ell_{i} to RR with C=4C=4.

Fitting the turns.

For both learners, three rules decide how the trainer fits a turn. For the policy gradient, the first rule applies only to turns with positive weights. A turn with a negative weight keeps all of its tokens. First, with the belief term, a fitted turn trains its whole text only when its belief line is verified. The belief line must satisfy S⁡(β,b)≥S⁡(β∗,b)−0.1S(\beta;b)\geq S(\beta^{*};b)-0.1. Otherwise, its belief-line tokens are not counted and its reasoning gets weight 0. The turn then trains its accepted action alone, with the reasoning and the line kept as context. With the action term alone, every fitted turn trains its whole text. Second, a turn has two blocks of tokens, the reasoning and the decision. Each block takes its own gradient step with its own clip of the gradient norm. The objective and its minimizer stay the same. The split keeps the long and noisy gradient of the reasoning from setting the pace of the short decision block. Third, the likelihood πϕ\pi_{\phi} uses the sampler of the policy. For the reasoning, it uses the sampling temperature, the top-pp and top-kk cuts and the presence penalty. For the decision, it uses the same temperature and presence penalty with no cut. Under a cut, the likelihood of a token is its tempered probability renormalized over the kept tokens. The sampled token always counts as kept. The fixed point is thus the policy used by the agent.

Histories and sample sets.

In phase kk, the teacher action replaces the agent action with probability ξk=ξ0​γk\xi_{k}=\xi_{0}\,\gamma^{k}. As in DAgger (Ross et al., 2011), the share of teacher actions in μk\mu_{k} thus decreases with kk. In our runs of two phases, the probability ξk\xi_{k} falls from 0.5 to 0.465, and in the five phases on Qwen3.5-4B to 0.374. On half of the training scenes, one more episode starts with random evidence actions. Because qkq_{k} does not change inside a phase, the samples of πk\pi_{k} stay valid for all of its updates. One sample set of HH histories thus serves the whole phase. Following the dynamic sampling of DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), we draw the batches in random passes and only from histories that give a gradient. These are the histories in which one of the agent’s own turns has an accepted action.

Step limit.

The M-step fits only a few samples of qkq_{k} at each history. It can thus also fit their noise. To limit this, the trainer computes KL(πk∥πϕ)\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{k}\,\|\,\pi_{\phi}) after each update. It computes this KL exactly at every position of the probe turns, which are turns of πk\pi_{k} from the first batch of the phase:

Δk​(ϕ)=1|𝒫|​∑p∈𝒫∑vπk​(v∣x<p)​log⁡πk​(v∣x<p)πϕ​(v∣x<p)≤ε,\Delta_{k}(\phi)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{v}\pi_{k}(v\mid x_{<p})\log\frac{\pi_{k}(v\mid x_{<p})}{\pi_{\phi}(v\mid x_{<p})}\leq\varepsilon, (16)

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the set of token positions of the probe turns, x<px_{<p} is the prefix before position pp, and vv runs over the vocabulary at the sampling temperature. When Δk>ε\Delta_{k}>\varepsilon, the phase stops. The model after that update is πk+1\pi_{k+1}. This rule follows the early stop of PPO implementations at 1.5 times a target KL (Schulman et al., 2017; Achiam, 2018) and the KL limit in the M-step of MPO (Abdolmaleki et al., 2018).

C.2 The EM learner

Algorithm 2 gives all the steps of RLVB with the EM learner.

Bayes view.

Let OO be the event “the teacher accepts the turn”, with p⁡(O∣h,x)=eR⁡(h,x)/αp(O\mid h,x)=e^{R(h,x)/\alpha}. This is a probability because R≤0R\leq 0. Then qk​(x∣h)=p⁡(x∣h,O)q_{k}(x\mid h)=p(x\mid h,O) under the prior πk\pi_{k}. The E-step is Bayes’ rule, and the M-step is the M-step of EM (Dempster et al., 1977).

Factors of qq.

RR depends on the decision dd only. Thus

qk​(z,β,u∣h)∝\displaystyle q_{k}(z,\beta,u\mid h)\;\propto πk​(z∣h)⏟reasoning⋅πk​(β∣h,z)​eRβ​(β,b)/α⏟belief line\displaystyle\underbrace{\pi_{k}(z\mid h)}_{\text{reasoning}}\ \cdot\ \underbrace{\pi_{k}(\beta\mid h,z)\,e^{R_{\beta}(\beta;b)/\alpha}}_{\text{belief line}} (17)
⋅πk​(u∣h,z,β)​π∗​(u∣b)1/α⏟action,\displaystyle\cdot\ \underbrace{\pi_{k}(u\mid h,z,\beta)\,\pi^{*}(u\mid b)^{1/\alpha}}_{\text{action}},

with Rβ=Sdec+η⁡(S+W)R_{\beta}=S_{\text{dec}}+\eta\,(S+W) the belief term of equation 5. For the action, with α=1\alpha=1, qkq_{k} is the normalized product of the policy and the teacher policy. With the action term alone, Rβ=0R_{\beta}=0. A line then gains weight only through the actions that follow it. With the belief term, qkq_{k} also moves the policy toward lines with a high belief score. For the reasoning, qk(z∣h)∝πk(z∣h)𝔼d∼πk(⋅∣h,z)[eR⁡(h,d)/α]q_{k}(z\mid h)\propto\pi_{k}(z\mid h)\,\mathbb{E}_{d\sim\pi_{k}(\cdot\mid h,z)}[e^{R(h,d)/\alpha}]. Thus no teacher text is a target for zz.

The M-step.

The M-step projects qkq_{k} onto the model class by a weighted maximum likelihood on the samples of the agent:

πk+1\displaystyle\pi_{k+1} =argminϕ𝔼hKL(qk(⋅∣h)∥πϕ(⋅∣h))\displaystyle=\arg\min_{\phi}\ \mathbb{E}_{h}\,\mathrm{KL}\big(q_{k}(\cdot\mid h)\,\|\,\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid h)\big) (18)
≈arg⁡maxϕ​∑h∑i=1Nw^i​log⁡πϕ​(xi∣h).\displaystyle\approx\arg\max_{\phi}\ \textstyle\sum_{h}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{w}_{i}\,\log\pi_{\phi}(x_{i}\mid h).

The trainer draws JJ turns from the weights by systematic resampling (Kitagawa, 1996) and fits each draw with the weight 1/J1/J. The expected gradient is then that of the weighted loss. The weights are not negative and sum to 1 at each history. The probability of a turn with a small weight goes down only because the probabilities sum to 1. The update thus needs no critic and no group baseline.

Mirror descent.

The prior πk\pi_{k} stays fixed for the updates of phase kk. Then πk+1=πϕ\pi_{k+1}=\pi_{\phi}. Phase 0 uses the base model π0\pi_{0}. If each projection is exact and RR is fixed,

πk∝πk−1​eR/α⇒πk∝π0​ek​R/α,πk​(u∣h,z,β)∝π0​(u∣h,z,β)​π∗​(u∣b)k/α.\begin{gathered}\pi_{k}\;\propto\;\pi_{k-1}\,e^{R/\alpha}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\pi_{k}\;\propto\;\pi_{0}\,e^{kR/\alpha},\\ \pi_{k}(u\mid h,z,\beta)\;\propto\;\pi_{0}(u\mid h,z,\beta)\;\pi^{*}(u\mid b)^{\,k/\alpha}.\end{gathered} (19)

Phase kk thus has the effective temperature α/k\alpha/k. As kk increases, the policy moves to the maximizers of RR. These are the teacher’s best action, and also the exact line β∗\beta^{*} with the belief term. In practice, RR is not fixed, because ρ^\hat{\rho} is measured again at every update. In addition, μk\mu_{k} changes from phase to phase. Equation 19 thus describes the ideal case. Each phase is a mirror-descent step on RR, as in policy mirror descent (Lan, 2023; Tomar et al., 2022). Unlike standard policy mirror descent, the step uses the teacher score RR in place of the Q-function of the current policy.

C.3 The policy-gradient learner

The policy gradient uses the histories, turns and rewards above. It replaces the weights of the E-step by those of equation 10. Let ri=R⁡(h,xi)+C​ℓir_{i}=R(h,x_{i})+C\ell_{i} be the reward of turn ii with its length term. At each history, we compute the advantages Ai=r~i−1N−1​∑j≠ir~jA_{i}=\tilde{r}_{i}-\tfrac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\tilde{r}_{j} over all of its sampled turns, the extra round included. Here r~i=max⁡(ri,maxj⁡rj−c)\tilde{r}_{i}=\max(r_{i},\max_{j}r_{j}-c) raises every reward to at least the best one minus c=20c=20 nats. A turn with a very low reward thus cannot raise the advantages of all the others. The advantages also stay in [−c,c][-c,c]. The weight of a turn is wi=s​Ai/Nw_{i}=sA_{i}/N, with one factor ss per mini-batch. We do not divide by the standard deviation of the group, because the rewards are already in nats. Dividing would also give large weights to a group of nearly equal rewards. A turn with a rejected action gets a weight of at most zero. Its probability can thus be lowered but never raised. As with the weights of EM, the factor ss makes the absolute weights of a mini-batch sum to the number of its histories with a target. This factor only balances the mini-batches, because we use Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) and clip the gradient norm of each block. Unlike EM, the policy gradient does not draw turns. It fits every turn with a nonzero weight. A phase uses its turns for several updates. A block with a positive weight therefore stops contributing once its mean log-ratio to πk\pi_{k} per counted token rises above log⁡(1+δ)\log(1+\delta). A block with a negative weight stops once this log-ratio falls below log⁡(1−δ)\log(1-\delta). We use δ=0.2\delta=0.2 and compute the log-ratio once per phase. This rule follows the clipped probability ratio of PPO (Schulman et al., 2017).

In our runs, the policy gradient fitted about 1,300 turns per update and EM about 300. This is because the policy gradient gives a weight to every sampled turn, and the draws of EM fall on the few turns of high reward. The steps of the policy gradient were also larger.

The reported runs of RLVB.

RLVB in table 1 is trained with the action term in equation 5 alone. As a result, the rules above for the belief term do not apply to it. They apply to RLVB (EM) and to the ablation runs with the belief term in table 5. For the two Qwen3-VL models, a phase has 25 updates and a sample set of 1,200 histories, of which 800 are used. The training takes 50 updates. Qwen3.5-4B learns faster. With phases of 25 updates, its reasoning became very short. We therefore give it a new sample set of 240 histories every 5 updates, of which 160 are used. We train it for 25 updates with no length reward. Section C.4 describes three more rules in the reward that we tested on Qwen3.5-4B.

C.4 Rules against steps without evidence

Why we tested the rules.

With phases of 5 updates, the agent of Qwen3.5-4B learned a second way to delay its answer. It took steps that bring no evidence, such as turning on the spot in MiniGrid. The action term lets such a step pass. In the teacher’s score, a step that brings no evidence costs only its time discount, which is 0.2 nats in most tasks and 0.5 nats in MineSweeper. The acceptance rule accepts every turn whose score is within log⁡20=3.0\log 20=3.0 nats of the teacher’s best action. A step without evidence is therefore still accepted. The measured answer accuracy ρ^\hat{\rho} of equation 12 can add to this. Where the agent’s answers are often wrong, ρ^\hat{\rho} is low. Answering then has a low value, and the teacher itself asks for more steps.

The three rules.

All three rules change the reward of the action term, and all three are computed from the exact posterior.

  1. 1.

    Exact answer accuracy. The estimate φ^\hat{\varphi} of equation 12 stays at its prior mean of 1, so ρ^​(b)=bmax\hat{\rho}(b)=b_{\max}. This is the accuracy of an agent that always reads its evidence correctly. The teacher’s choice between a step and an answer then depends on the evidence alone and not on the agent’s own errors.

  2. 2.

    A cap on steps without evidence. An illegal action gets a teacher score of at most the best action’s score minus 3.5 nats. So does a step that brings no expected evidence and is not one of the teacher’s best steps. The acceptance rule therefore rejects both. The teacher’s own moves in the training games follow the same capped scores.

  3. 3.

    The teacher’s turn as a positive example. With the cap, more histories have no accepted turn of the agent. At such a history, the update can only lower the probability of the agent’s turns. We then add the teacher’s own belief line and action to the turns of this history as a positive example.

Results.

We trained Qwen3.5-4B with the three rules in the same way as the reported run, with phases of 5 updates and 25 updates, and we tested it on the same three test seeds. Table 12 compares the two runs. With the rules, the accuracy is 1.6% higher on HiddenGames, 0.2% lower on Pro-Worlds and 2.9% higher on RoboQuest. In a paired test over the test games, only the gain on RoboQuest is significant (p=0.014p=0.014). On the HiddenGames tasks with an answer, a larger share of the steps adds evidence, 28.0% compared to 21.2%, and the agent takes fewer steps per episode. Fewer episodes end without an answer on all three benchmarks, for example 6.0% compared to 11.6% on Pro-Worlds. On HiddenGames and Pro-Worlds, the agent reaches sufficient evidence about as often as without the rules. On RoboQuest, it answers with sufficient evidence in 71.3% of the episodes, compared to 68.8%. We report the run without the rules in table 1, so that all three models are trained with the same reward.

C.5 One family of weights

The two weightings are two limits of one family. Let r1,…,rNr_{1},\ldots,r_{N} be the rewards of the turns at a history, r¯\bar{r} their mean, and ωiα=eri/α/∑jerj/α\omega_{i}^{\alpha}=e^{r_{i}/\alpha}/\sum_{j}e^{r_{j}/\alpha} the EM weights at temperature α\alpha, without the acceptance rule.

Proposition 3.

(i) As α→0\alpha\to 0, ωα\omega^{\alpha} puts all of its weight on the turns of highest reward. (ii) As α→∞\alpha\to\infty, α⁡(ωiα−1/N)→(ri−r¯)/N\alpha\,(\omega_{i}^{\alpha}-1/N)\to(r_{i}-\bar{r})/N. (iii) The leave-one-out advantage is ri−1N−1​∑j≠irj=NN−1​(ri−r¯)r_{i}-\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j\neq i}r_{j}=\frac{N}{N-1}(r_{i}-\bar{r}).

Proof.

For (i), ωiα/ωjα=e(ri−rj)/α\omega_{i}^{\alpha}/\omega_{j}^{\alpha}=e^{(r_{i}-r_{j})/\alpha} tends to 00 whenever ri<rjr_{i}<r_{j}. For (ii), er/α=1+r/α+O⁡(α−2)e^{r/\alpha}=1+r/\alpha+O(\alpha^{-2}), which gives ωiα=(1+(ri−r¯)/α)/N+O⁡(α−2)\omega_{i}^{\alpha}=\big(1+(r_{i}-\bar{r})/\alpha\big)/N+O(\alpha^{-2}). For (iii), ∑j≠irj=N​r¯−ri\sum_{j\neq i}r_{j}=N\bar{r}-r_{i}. ∎

By (ii) and (iii), the weights of the policy gradient at each history are limα→∞α⁡(ωiα−1/N)\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}\alpha\,(\omega_{i}^{\alpha}-1/N) times the positive factor s​N/(N−1)sN/(N-1). This holds without the floor, the limit cc and the acceptance rule. The policy gradient thus uses the centered EM weights ωiα−1/N\omega_{i}^{\alpha}-1/N at high temperature. EM uses the uncentered weights. At the first update of a phase, πϕ=πk\pi_{\phi}=\pi_{k} and 𝔼x∼πk​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​(x∣h)]=0\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\pi_{k}}\big[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}(x\mid h)\big]=0. The centered and the uncentered weights thus give the same expected gradient of equation 9. Their steps differ by a term of mean zero. By (i), EM at a low temperature fits only the best turn of each history, as rejection-sampling fine-tuning does (Zelikman et al., 2022). Our EM uses α=1\alpha=1. At this temperature, eRe^{R} is the teacher’s probability of approving the turn.

The two learners differ in how far they move from πk\pi_{k} on the same turns. The EM weights are non-negative and sum to one at each history. The loss of equation 9 is thus smallest when πϕ\pi_{\phi} matches them on the sampled turns. The fit then settles near qkq_{k}. The policy gradient also has negative weights, which keep lowering the probability of poor turns. Only the ratio clip and the step limit of equation 16 bound its steps.

Appendix D What the lookahead adds

To see what the lookahead adds without training a model, we play the 756 test games of HiddenGames with the teacher alone. The teacher knows the exact posterior and answers like a perfect answerer. Its ρ^\hat{\rho} therefore stays at its prior. It takes the action of highest value. Table 14 compares the step chosen by the lookahead with a random legal step. Both rules stop at the same point, where the teacher would answer.

As table 14 shows, the lookahead matters where the steps differ in what they reveal. In MineSweeper, MiniGrid, FrozenLake and Sokoban, random steps lose most games. In MineSweeper, every failure is a revealed mine. Every step in the Tabletop tasks splits the possible answers in the same way. The choice of step thus does not matter there. A lookahead of depth 1 gives the same result as depth 2. With a perfect answerer, the teacher answers exactly when the posterior identifies the answer. It does so in all 500 games with an answer action. Answering at the first turn instead solves 18.0% of these games. With a less reliable answerer, ρ^\hat{\rho} lowers the value of answering. As appendix A shows, the teacher then asks for more evidence before it answers.

Appendix E Benchmarks in detail

HiddenGames.

HiddenGames is a mixture of seven tasks from different agent benchmarks. In each task, the agent must find a hidden target from what it observes. MineSweeper (Wang et al., 2026a) hides the mines of a small board. In MiniGrid KeyCorridor (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2023), the agent must find the room that holds the key. In FrozenLake (Wang et al., 2025a), we hide the goal and the distant holes. In Sokoban (Wang et al., 2025a), we hide the target square. The agent must thus explore before it can plan. The three Tabletop tasks are rendered scenes of a table (Tao et al., 2025). The agent must find which button lights which lamp, which cup hides a named object as in figure 1, or which block slides farther. It sees only two camera images after each action. The environment of every task knows the prior and the likelihood of each observation. The teacher of section 3.2 can thus compute the exact posterior. We train and test on all seven tasks. The test split consists of 756 games whose seeds, maps and Tabletop colors are never seen in training.

Pro-Worlds.

We introduce Pro-Worlds, a benchmark of how visual agents gather, retain and combine evidence before they commit to an answer. Each game hides one of a few answers, for example which emotion a face shows or which fish a picture shows. The game draws its world as a grid of sites, each a tile of 16×1616\times 16 color cells. The agent sees one site at a time through a window, rendered as a 256×256256\times 256 picture. At each turn, the agent either moves the window by one site with ACTION: MOVE UP, DOWN, LEFT or RIGHT, or submits an answer with ACTION: SUBMIT. A move at the edge keeps the window in place but still counts. A play allows at most 35 moves. It ends with a submission, with a move when no moves are left, or after 43 turns. The prompt gives the rules of the game, the list of answers and every picture seen so far with its position. We place the start where the first view never decides the answer.

The engine knows every possible world of a game and can thus compute the exact posterior. This posterior holds the worlds consistent with every site seen so far, with the same prior weight for each answer. As in the other benchmarks, a submission is premature when the posterior of the top answer is below 0.95. Table 14 lists the 15 test games. We test on 20 plays of each game, 300 plays in all. Eight of the games are the training games of the benchmark, drawn at random from the 15. However, no model in this paper trains on Pro-Worlds.

RoboQuest.

RoboQuest (Liu et al., 2026) consists of ten mobile manipulation tasks built around search, inspection and interactive testing. In each task, such as finding the odd parcel by weighing, the agent must gather information through physical interaction before it decides to finish. Liu et al. report that agents often stop exploring too early (Liu et al., 2026). Unlike the other two benchmarks, RoboQuest runs in a physics simulator of real kitchens. Its possible states cannot be listed, and there is no exact posterior. Many of its answers are also actions in the scene rather than a choice among listed options. The belief lines of all agents are therefore free text, such as Possible: blue water bottle may be in drawer 2 or another compartment. We use RoboQuest to test whether what an agent learns from exact posteriors transfers to a task without one. We use the text version of its decision-level setting, where the agent chooses high-level actions and scripted helpers carry them out. We test on 50 games of each task, 500 games in all.

Appendix F Results per task

Tables 17, 16 and 15 break down the accuracy of table 1 by task. A learner of RLVB is the best method in five of the seven HiddenGames tasks, 14 of the 15 Pro-Worlds games, and 9 of the 10 RoboQuest tasks. On HiddenGames, the largest gains of RLVB over Base occur in the Tabletop tasks, with 51.0% on lamps and 34.8% on cups, while on RoboQuest the largest gains occur in the search tasks, with 39.6% on Search Room and 55.5% on Blackout Search. On Pro-Worlds, RLVB reaches 30.2% on both the seen and the unseen games, compared to 17.9% and 16.9% for Base.

Appendix G The posterior teacher on every task

Every task has its own teacher. The value, the lookahead and the choice between answering and taking a step are the same in all tasks. Each teacher uses the posterior of its own task. Table 18 gives the accuracy of each teacher alone with the exact posterior and a perfect answerer, as in the reference row of table 1. In MineSweeper, every failure of the teacher is a revealed mine. In Sokoban, its two failures used up the move budget. The teacher of Pro-Worlds builds the posterior of each game from its game engine. RoboQuest has no exact posterior and thus no teacher. It tests whether what RLVB learns transfers to a task without one.

Appendix H Settings of the RLVB runs

Shared configuration.

All methods share one configuration for each model. Every run of every method caps the reasoning at 8,192 tokens in training and in testing. Each run also samples with the settings of table 20. Each run trained on one node with 8 GPUs, either H200 GPUs with 141 GB or A100 GPUs with 80 GB.

Appendix I The PPO (belief + action) baseline

PPO (belief + action) states a belief before each action. An LLM judge rewards this belief at every turn. A turn consists of the reasoning, a belief state and an action. The belief state is a list of bullet points inside <belief_state> tags, each with one word of certainty such as confirmed, probable or ruled out. The action is inside <action> tags. The turn receives the same input as the other methods, with the rules of the task, the actions and observations so far and the current observation. It also receives the belief state of the previous turn.

The belief reward of a turn is Rb=f⁡(st+sc+d+o)/4R_{b}=f\,(s_{t}+s_{c}+d+o)/4. Here ff scores the format of the belief state by the number of bullets, a certainty word in each bullet, no repeats and the length. The judge score sts_{t} measures whether the new belief state takes in the newest observation. The judge score scs_{c} measures whether its claims are true. dd is the entropy of the certainty words, and oo is the outcome reward. To score scs_{c}, the judge checks the claims against a text description of the true hidden state. Only the judge sees this description. The judge is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at temperature 0, without thinking. A failed judge call receives the batch mean of its term.

The tokens of the belief state are trained on RbR_{b}, normalized over the belief states of the batch. The reasoning and action tokens are trained with PPO on the outcome reward 0.999t⋅𝟙​[correct]0.999^{t}\cdot\mathbb{1}[\text{correct}]. PPO uses a learned value function and GAE (Schulman et al., 2016) with γ=λ=1\gamma=\lambda=1. Training uses LoRA with rank 16 and alpha 32, a learning rate of 10−510^{-5} and 50 updates of 16 episodes each, with no warm start. At test time, the prompt keeps the rules of the belief state but drops the list of task-specific fields and the format example used in training.

Appendix J Settings of the baselines

Table 20 gives the settings of the trained baselines, which are all action-only. They train LoRA adapters for 50 updates on the training split of HiddenGames, with the sampling settings and the thinking budget of table 20. GRPO and PPO train with verl (Sheng et al., 2025). SFT trains on the teacher’s action in its winning games, after the base model’s own reasoning. Its learning rate follows a cosine schedule with 10 warm-up steps.

Appendix K Why RLVB works: details

This section provides the details and additional tests underlying section 4.6. Unless a table or figure states otherwise, all numbers are for Qwen3-VL-4B.

Measures.

A step refers to a move on Pro-Worlds, a lift or press in the Tabletop tasks, and an action such as opening a drawer or weighing two parcels on RoboQuest. A step adds evidence when it changes the exact posterior or, on RoboQuest, when it meets a new evidence requirement of the task, such as the agent now seeing a target object. On HiddenGames, we use the five tasks with an answer: the three Tabletop tasks, MiniGrid, and MineSweeper. On RoboQuest, requirements can be counted in eight of the ten tasks, so we omit Stamps and Puzzle Box from these measures. The chance of a correct answer is the exact posterior of the top answer, representing the accuracy of an agent that reads its evidence without error.

Reading the belief lines on RoboQuest.

On RoboQuest, belief lines are free text. The task has no posterior. We read every belief line in the test episodes of Base (w/ belief) and RLVB on the 361 of 400 instances that at least one method solves. These are 56,556 lines from the three models and three test seeds. Language-model readers judge each line against the trace of an episode that solved the same instance. The readers do not see which agent wrote the line. They record whether the line names a single answer or leaves part of the answer open. They also record whether it keeps the true answer. When the agent submits at that turn, they record whether the submission gives the answer that the line names. A second reader labels 2,595 of these lines. It agrees on whether the line names a single answer for 2,539 of them, on whether it keeps the true answer for 2,514, and on whether the submission gives the named answer for 2,562.

K.1 The evidence at the answer

The evidence at the answer for each model.

Figure 10 repeats figure 5 for each of the three models and adds RLVB (EM). Across every model and benchmark, RLVB gives fewer answers at low levels of evidence and more answers with sufficient evidence than Base. Table 21 reports the split from equation 11 for RLVB and PPO (belief + action) on each model, with 95% intervals from a bootstrap over the test games. For RLVB, the part from answering with more evidence is positive on every model and benchmark, while the part from accuracy at the same evidence is negative or not different from zero. This second part is most negative in HiddenGames on the two Qwen3-VL models (−7.9-7.9 and −12.9-12.9%), because after training these models are less often correct with sufficient evidence in the Tabletop tasks. For PPO (belief + action), the second part is positive on RoboQuest, at +2.8+2.8% over the three models.

Answers with sufficient evidence.

Answers with sufficient evidence might be correct more often only because they come from easier games. Table 22 tests this by comparing the two kinds of answers within the same test game. For each model, it uses the games that have both kinds of answers across all methods and test episodes. Within the same game, answers with sufficient evidence are correct 49.5 to 76.1% more often than answers with insufficient evidence. This also holds for Base’s episodes alone and for RLVB’s episodes alone. Most MiniGrid and MineSweeper games are not part of this test because no method reaches sufficient evidence in them. The lower part of table 22 gives the share of episodes in which an agent gives a correct answer with sufficient evidence. RLVB’s share is 4.5 times Base’s share on HiddenGames, 26 times on Pro-Worlds, and 2.1 times on RoboQuest. Compared to Base (w/ belief), its share is 2.3, 7.8, and 1.7 times as large.

K.2 When the agents commit

Figure 11 shows the turn at which the agent commits in each episode, relative to the first turn with sufficient evidence. On Qwen3-VL-4B, RLVB commits within one step of that turn in 46% of HiddenGames episodes and 67% of RoboQuest episodes, compared with 7% and 31% for Base.

Steps, useful steps and sufficient evidence for every method.

Table 23 reports, for each model and six methods, the steps per episode, the share of steps that add evidence, the share of episodes reaching sufficient evidence, and the share of turns on which the agent answers. It also includes the on-policy variant of RLVB from appendix L.

Episodes without an answer.

Table 24 summarizes the episodes that end without an answer. On the Tabletop tasks, every such episode has sufficient evidence (5 of 5 for RLVB and 63 of 63 for the on-policy variant). The model finished the work, but it did not answer. In MiniGrid and MineSweeper, almost none of these episodes have sufficient evidence (1 of 83 and 1 of 186). The steps there did not bring the needed evidence. On RoboQuest, forcing an answer at the last turn of these episodes solves 3 of 38 episodes for RLVB and 21 of 98 for the on-policy variant. Working longer fails in two ways. In MiniGrid and MineSweeper, the steps bring no evidence. In the Tabletop tasks, the model does not act on its evidence. The on-policy variant shows both failures more often than RLVB.

Intervals and commits by belief line.

Table 26 reports the 95% intervals for the differences in table 8. For all task groups, table 25 reports the commit rates by belief line and evidence. Outside the Tabletop tasks, RLVB also commits less often than Base (w/ belief) when its belief line names a single answer while several remain. RLVB commits on 6.5 to 55.9% of these turns, while Base (w/ belief) commits on 61.3 to 74.3% of them.

Table 27 compares the belief lines after the same number of steps instead of at the same states. Table 28 reports how well the belief line separates turns with sufficient evidence from turns where several answers remain. Table 29 evaluates the belief line across all turns. Over all turns, the belief line of RLVB is more exact in the Tabletop tasks but less exact on Pro-Worlds, because RLVB spends many turns in later states that Base (w/ belief) rarely reaches.

Table 30 examines what the belief line states when agents fail. On Pro-Worlds, most early commits by Base (w/ belief) come with a belief line that still names several answers. On the Tabletop tasks, 38 to 72% of its early commits occur with an overconfident belief line. In HiddenGames, most early commits by RLVB likewise occur with an overconfident belief line. On Pro-Worlds, almost all early commits of RLVB with a belief line that names several answers happen at the limit of 35 moves, in 219 of 244, 536 of 553 and 668 of 671 cases, against at most 4.3% for Base (w/ belief). Among wrong answers given with sufficient evidence, the belief line excludes the true answer in 71 to 97% of cases across every agent and model with ten or more such answers, and the answer contradicts a correct belief line in at most one case per model.

Following the belief line or the posterior.

At every turn, we compute the posterior teacher’s action twice, once from the exact posterior and once from the belief line. In the second case, we read the belief line as the set of answers it names. The two actions differ most at turns where the belief line is wrong about the answer. Table 31 reports the percentage of these turns where the agent follows the belief line and the percentage where it follows the posterior. When the belief line names a single answer under insufficient evidence, Base (w/ belief) follows the belief line and commits on 71.6 to 99.4% of these turns. RLVB commits on 9.8 to 81.4% of these turns and takes the best step under the posterior on 18.6 to 56.5%. When there is sufficient evidence and the belief line still names several answers, RLVB follows the belief line and keeps working on 75.6 to 99.0% of Tabletop turns and 44.1 to 55.2% of Pro-Worlds turns. Base (w/ belief) does this on 6.2 to 46.5% of Tabletop turns. RLVB therefore follows its belief line when the belief line names several answers, while Base (w/ belief) often commits against it. When there is sufficient evidence and its belief line names a single wrong answer, RLVB commits to this answer on 62.3 to 76.7% of these Tabletop turns. This turns the misreading into a wrong answer. By contrast, the agents’ steps do not closely follow the belief line or the posterior. On Pro-Worlds, before there is sufficient evidence, a step by either agent is a best step under the belief line or under the posterior only 5.6 to 9.5% more often than a random legal step. There is no difference between the two agents. Finally, we exclude MineSweeper turns where the belief line names a mine set that has already been ruled out. We cannot read such a belief line as a belief.

K.3 The value of a step

Random steps up to the limit.

To see what the task alone determines, we first run every test scene without a model, taking a random step at each turn until no steps remain. Table 32 shows the result, where an episode ended by a step, as in MineSweeper, counts as wrong from that step onward. In the Tabletop tasks, every step rules out some answers, and three to five steps identify the answer in every scene. On Pro-Worlds, each step is also safe, but evidence accumulates slowly: after all 35 steps, the chance of a correct answer grows only from 13% to 28%, with sufficient evidence reached in 2% of scenes. In MiniGrid, the 64 random steps identify the answer in only 18% of scenes, while the posterior teacher identifies it in every scene in 8.3 steps; the evidence therefore exists, but only well-chosen steps reach it. In MineSweeper, a step can even end the episode, because opening a cell with a mine loses the game. Finally, on RoboQuest, the steps consist of a limited number of robot actions, some of which cannot be undone.

Evidence within the reach of Base.

Base answers early. We test whether the evidence it needed was out of its reach. We replay each Base test episode on Qwen3-VL-4B using Base’s steps up to the turn when it answers. From that state, we take random steps without a model until the task allows no more steps. Table 33 gives the result. On the Tabletop tasks, sufficient evidence is present in 11% of episodes when Base answers, and in all of them after the random steps. On Pro-Worlds, the chance of a correct answer grows from 20% to 31%. In these tasks, Base could have gathered the evidence in the same episode by not answering yet. In MiniGrid and MineSweeper, random steps reach sufficient evidence in only 18% and 9% of episodes. Random steps from the start of the game reach it just as rarely there, as table 32 shows.

Steps against random steps.

Table 34 compares each agent with random steps in the same scene. The random steps stop after the same number of steps that the agent takes in that episode. As a result, the agent and the random steps differ only in which steps they take. On the Tabletop tasks, both agents’ steps reach sufficient evidence somewhat more often than random steps. The increase is 5.0 to 16.0% for RLVB and 1.5 to 11.5% for Base (w/ belief). On Pro-Worlds, RLVB’s steps reach sufficient evidence in 9.6 to 14.4% of episodes, compared to 1.8 to 2.3% for random steps. The main difference between the two agents is the number of steps. On the Tabletop tasks, RLVB takes 2.6 to 3.1 steps per episode, while Base (w/ belief) takes 0.3 to 1.9.

The value of a step on all states.

Figure 7 shows the value of one step across four step windows. Table 35 reports the underlying numbers and adds MiniGrid and MineSweeper. We follow every episode from the start of its game, which is the same state for all methods, and average the value of one step over all games in which a method takes a step in that window. On the Tabletop tasks, Pro-Worlds, and RoboQuest, the value of a step differs little across methods in every window, and where differences appear, RLVB is neither consistently lower nor consistently higher than Base. In MiniGrid and MineSweeper, the first step of RLVB is worth 0.14% compared to 1.24% for Base, while its steps after the fourth remain at 0.2 to 0.3%. On the games where every method takes a step in the window, the differences between RLVB and PPO (belief + action) are not significant on Pro-Worlds or RoboQuest in any window except the first step on RoboQuest, where the difference is 0.6%. On these games, RLVB trails Base on RoboQuest by 2.2 and 1.7% in the last two windows, which contain only the games where Base is still taking steps that late.

Across states reached by both Base (w/ belief) and RLVB (where a state consists of the game and the number of answers still possible), we also compare the steps taken with an exact belief line. A step taken by RLVB raises the posterior of the correct answer by 0.9% more than a step taken by Base (w/ belief) on the Tabletop tasks (95% interval from −2.6-2.6 to +3.8+3.8%) and by 0.02% less on Pro-Worlds (from −0.08-0.08 to +0.07+0.07%). Within each agent, a step taken with an exact belief line and a step taken with a misread line at the same state differ by 1.6% or less on the Tabletop tasks and by 0.17% or less on Pro-Worlds. We also let the posterior teacher continue playing from each of these steps until it commits, counting how many more steps it needs than it does after its own best step at the same state. With an exact belief line, a step from RLVB costs the teacher 0.02 fewer steps than one from Base (w/ belief) on Pro-Worlds (95% interval from −0.16-0.16 to +0.13+0.13, with about 0.6 such steps for both agents) and 0.004 fewer in the Tabletop tasks (from −0.03-0.03 to +0.02+0.02), where every step is a best step of the teacher. Only in MiniGrid and MineSweeper does a step from RLVB cost more, by 0.53 steps (from +0.37+0.37 to +0.70+0.70). Within each agent, the difference between steps taken with an exact belief line and those with a misread belief line has an interval that includes zero across all three groups of tasks.

The value of a step from shared states.

We repeat this comparison starting from states shared by the methods. A shared state is the same test game with the same amount of evidence that Base, PPO (belief + action), and RLVB all reach (possibly via different preceding steps) and from which each takes a step. We track each agent’s subsequent steps across four windows: the first step, steps 2 to 4, steps 5 to 7, and the later steps. The value of a step is how much it raises the exact posterior of the correct answer, or on RoboQuest the share of requirements met. We first evaluate the value of one step in a window across states where every method takes a step in that window. On the first step, all three methods achieve similar value: for Base, PPO (belief + action), and RLVB, it raises the posterior by 15.6, 14.9, and 14.8% in HiddenGames and by 1.5, 1.9, and 1.5% on Pro-Worlds, and meets 19.1, 19.3, and 19.8% of the requirements on RoboQuest. On RoboQuest, a step by Base and a step by RLVB also have similar value in later windows, with 15.8 and 16.9% in steps 2 to 4, 12.8 and 12.1% in steps 5 to 7, and 17.7 and 16.8% in the later steps. In HiddenGames, a step by RLVB in steps 2 to 4 is worth 24.9% compared to 21.7% for Base, while on Pro-Worlds a later step by RLVB is worth 1.0% compared to 1.3 to 1.5% for Base. We then measure the total increase since the shared state, where an agent that has committed keeps its value. Even so, this increase is larger for RLVB than for Base because RLVB continues taking steps in later windows where Base has already committed. For Base, PPO (belief + action), and RLVB, the increase reaches 44.6, 59.5, and 70.1% on RoboQuest, 23.6, 38.6, and 43.7% in HiddenGames, and 7.6, 12.0, and 22.2% on Pro-Worlds. In steps 2 to 4, for example, RLVB takes a step from 83% of the shared states in HiddenGames and 81% on RoboQuest, compared to 26% and 64% for Base.

Actions against the best action.

To test whether training alters action selection, we compare each chosen action against the best actions available in that state, as ranked by the posterior teacher. We evaluate on Pro-Worlds and HiddenGames excluding the Tabletop tasks, where all valid actions have equal value under the teacher. Because RoboQuest has no teacher, we instead measure the share of actions that meet one more requirement. A random action is a best action in 33% of HiddenGames states and 44% of Pro-Worlds states. Every method selects a best action more often than a random action, exceeding random by 2 to 7% in HiddenGames and by 8 to 10% on Pro-Worlds, with all differences significant.

RLVB and Base select a best action at similar rates. In HiddenGames, the share is 40% for RLVB and 37% for Base, a small difference of 2.5% (95% interval from 1.2 to 3.9%). On Pro-Worlds, the corresponding shares are 53% and 52%, with an interval for the difference that includes zero (from −0.5-0.5 to +1.5+1.5%). Across the HiddenGames tasks, the difference runs in both directions: RLVB exceeds Base in FrozenLake (43% versus 39%), falls below Base in MineSweeper (39% versus 47%), and matches Base in MiniGrid and Sokoban.

As a second measure, we evaluate the value of the chosen action relative to the best action. Although the share of best moves does not differ on Pro-Worlds, the value of the chosen move is significantly lower for RLVB by 3.0% (62.8% of the best move’s value compared to 65.8% for Base). In MiniGrid, the chosen action falls 0.21 to 0.23 nats below the best action across all methods, while in MineSweeper it falls 0.99 nats below for RLVB compared to 0.55 for Base and 1.45 for PPO (belief + action). Both measures show only small differences in either direction, so training has little effect on action choice.

K.4 The check in the harness

Table 36 reports the accuracy of Base and RLVB with and without the check described in section 4.6. It also reports how often the agent keeps working after the check and how useful its further steps are. The check also helps RLVB on RoboQuest and raises its accuracy by 1.9 to 7.7%. On Qwen3.5-4B with the check, RLVB reaches 61.7%, while Base reaches 50.9%. On HiddenGames and Pro-Worlds, the check changes the accuracy of RLVB by at most 2.8%. On the Tabletop tasks, Base keeps working after the check in 17%, 2% and 3% of the checked episodes on Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B.

K.5 The on-policy variant

What the on-policy variant knows when it does not answer.

The exact posterior shows two cases among the episodes that the on-policy variant ends without an answer. In Tabletop Blocks, it gives no answer in 55 of 100 episodes, even though the evidence is sufficient in all of them, with a single answer remaining for four turns on average. Its belief line still names several blocks in 39 of these episodes and a wrong block in 16. In these episodes, the model’s reasoning is cut off at the limit of 8,192 tokens in 91% of turns with sufficient evidence, after which the model takes further steps instead of answering. Across the Tabletop tasks, it answers in 69% of turns with sufficient evidence when its reasoning finishes within the limit (58% for RLVB), but in only 22% when its reasoning is cut off (43% for RLVB). In MiniGrid, by contrast, it gives no answer in 90 of 100 episodes, where the evidence is not sufficient because three answers remain possible in 89 of them after all 64 turns. Here the model is right that it does not know the answer, yet it still does not answer when no step is left.

A forced answer at the last turn.

For RoboQuest episodes that end without an answer, we test a simple rule: once the agent has used all its steps, we begin its reply as a submit so that the model only writes the answer. With this rule, the on-policy variant solves 21 of its 98 episodes without an answer, raising its accuracy on RoboQuest from 58.8% to 63.0%. The rule has almost no effect on Base, which ends at most 1 of 500 episodes without an answer.

Do the further steps of the on-policy variant bring evidence?

The on-policy variant ends many more episodes without an answer than RLVB. Table 37 tests whether its final turns in these episodes still add evidence, counting every turn (including rejected actions) as adding evidence whenever the exact posterior changes or, on RoboQuest, a new requirement is met. In MiniGrid, none of the last ten turns adds evidence in any of its 90 episodes without an answer; 89 of these episodes end after 64 turns at the starting posterior of one third. In MineSweeper, the last ten turns add no evidence in 94 of its 96 such episodes, compared to 44 of 81 for RLVB, whose last ten steps raise the posterior by 3.5% on average. On the Tabletop tasks, every episode of the on-policy variant without an answer already holds sufficient evidence (63 of 63) for 3.9 turns on average, and 152 of these 247 turns are rejected actions. On Pro-Worlds, both agents use all 35 moves in most episodes (86% and 69%), with 3.2% and 3.5% of their moves after the tenth still adding evidence, close to 4.2% for Base. Although RLVB ends no Pro-Worlds episode without an answer, ten turns without evidence are common there for every agent: the last ten turns before the answer add no evidence in 65% of episodes for RLVB, 68% of answered episodes for the on-policy variant, and 57% of those for Base (w/ belief). On RoboQuest, the two agents reach sufficient evidence about equally often (78% and 76%) and end only 2.8% and 1.2% of episodes without an answer.

K.6 Examples

Figure 12 shows episodes in which many steps yield little evidence. In episode A on Pro-Worlds, the agent takes all 35 steps in one corner of the board without seeing any site that reveals part of the picture, leaving all eight answers possible at the end. In episode B of the same task, it takes 21 steps, sees three such sites, and is left with a single answer. In the first Search Room episode on RoboQuest, the agent takes 29 steps and sees only one of the three objects; thirteen of these steps are not valid actions of the task. It then submits places for the other two objects without having seen them.

Appendix L Sampling in phases against on-policy sampling

As described in section 3, RLVB samples its training games only at the start of a phase and reuses them for all updates in that phase, while on-policy methods such as PPO play new games before every update. Because on-policy sampling is the more common choice, we also train an on-policy variant of RLVB on Qwen3-VL-4B. The only difference is that this variant samples a small set of new games before every update. Figure 13 compares the two approaches.

The first difference is cost: RLVB takes 6.4 hours in total, with its two sampling passes taking 47 and 74 minutes and each of its 50 updates then taking about 5 minutes. We stopped the on-policy variant after 46 updates, which took 20.8 hours. Because every update of the variant includes sampling, updates grow slower as training proceeds, averaging 20 minutes over the first ten updates and 39 minutes over the last ten. As the middle panel of figure 13 shows, the games sampled by the on-policy variant lengthen from about 5 turns in the first ten updates to about 20 in the last ten because the model answers less and less often. In contrast, the games sampled by RLVB have 5 turns in the first phase and 7.5 in the second.

The second difference is what the model learns. The on-policy variant’s longer training does not pay off. On the same test episodes, the variant falls behind RLVB on all three benchmarks (figure 13). The gap is 4.9% on HiddenGames, 0.6% on Pro-Worlds, and 1.6% on RoboQuest. The variant reaches sufficient evidence as often as RLVB, but it then often gives no answer (table 23). Its extra steps in MiniGrid and MineSweeper bring almost no evidence (table 37). A likely reason is the reward. It gives a very low value to an early answer, and it charges very little for one more step after the evidence is sufficient. Under on-policy sampling, each update draws its games from a model that already answers slightly less often than the previous one. The middle panel of figure 13 is consistent with this drift toward fewer answers. With phases, in contrast, the model playing the games is renewed only once during training. The on-policy variant’s reasoning is also cut off more often at the 8,192-token limit. After a cutoff, the variant mostly takes more steps instead of answering. We keep the phases because they take a third of the time and produce a model that ends fewer episodes without an answer. Section C.4 describes three more rules tested against steps that bring no evidence.

In the test episodes, the on-policy variant runs for too long. On Qwen3-VL-4B, it takes 18.9 steps per episode in the five HiddenGames tasks with an answer, compared to 7.9 for RLVB. It ends half of these episodes without an answer, compared to 18% for RLVB (table 24). It commits before its evidence is sufficient in only 7% of these episodes, compared to 28%. Unlike RLVB, it often keeps working after its belief line names a single answer (section 4.6). Table 37 shows what its extra steps add, and appendix K describes what it knows when it does not answer.

Appendix M A larger thinking budget

Every run caps the reasoning at 8,192 tokens. To see whether this cap makes the base models answer early, we also test Base with a cap of 16,384 tokens. Table 38 shows that the larger budget does not help. The accuracy changes by −0.4-0.4 to 2.6%, and none of these differences is significant. The base models therefore do not answer too early because their reasoning is cut.

Appendix N Two case studies

Case studies.

Table 39 shows two games of the cups task played by Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking. To show a typical case, we drew each game at random from a group of similar games. Beliefs in red drop an answer still allowed by the evidence. Figure 14 to figure 45 show one test episode of each task.

We drew the first game from the 28 of 100 test games where RLVB waits and answers correctly but Base (w/ belief) answers too early and wrongly. The agent must find the pink cylinder, which is under cup 1. Base (w/ belief) does not lift any cup. It writes that the cylinder is under cup 2 or 3, although it has no evidence against cups 1 and 4. It then submits cup 3. RLVB first lifts cup 2 and finds nothing. It then lifts cup 1 and finds the pink cylinder. Only then does it write that the answer is cup 1 and submit cup 1. After the first lift, its belief still names all four cups and is more cautious than needed. However, it never rules out a cup that could still hide the cylinder.

We drew the second game from the 13 games where RLVB answers wrongly although it had enough evidence. The agent must find the orange cylinder, which is under cup 4. The other cups hide orange cubes and an orange ball. RLVB lifts cups 1, 2 and 3 one by one. After each lift, its belief is correct. It then lifts cup 4 and sees the orange cylinder. The evidence now shows the answer. Yet it writes that only cup 5 is possible and submits cup 5. Its reasoning shows that it reads the object under cup 4 as a yellow cylinder. It writes “Cup 4: lifted, yellow cylinder →\rightarrow no”. RLVB thus stopped at the right time but misread the color of the object under cup 4.
